topics.title: 1.1.1 Discrete and Continuous Quantities
topics.learn: Everything around you that can be measured or counted is a quantity. Quantities come in two kinds. Discrete quantities are separate, countable items with specific values. You can count them one by one: 1, 2, 3 … There is nothing "in between". You cannot have 2.5 students in a classroom. Continuous quantities can take any value within a range. They flow smoothly without breaks. Water can be 30 °C, 30.5 °C, 30.51 °C, and so on — there is always another value in between.

topics.title: 1.1.2 Introduction to Digital Systems
topics.learn: A digital system is an electronic system that uses only two values: 0 and 1. These two values are called binary digits, or bits for short. Why only two values? Because it is easy for an electronic circuit to tell "voltage present" from "no voltage". Every number, letter, photo and song in a computer is finally stored as a long pattern of these bits. 0 represents OFF, LOW, or FALSE. 1 represents ON, HIGH, or TRUE.

topics.title: 1.1.3 Analog and Digital Signals
topics.learn: A signal is a changing voltage (or other quantity) that carries information. Analog signals are continuous signals that change smoothly over time, like a sine wave. Examples: the human voice, a traditional mercury thermometer. Digital signals have only two levels: HIGH (1) and LOW (0). They jump instantly between these values, which creates a square wave. Example: computer data.

topics.title: 1.1.4 Boolean Algebra
topics.learn: Boolean algebra was developed by the English mathematician George Boole. It is a kind of algebra that deals with only two values: TRUE (1) and FALSE (0). It is the foundation of digital electronics and computer programming — every if condition in a program is a small piece of Boolean algebra.

topics.title: 1.1.5 Boolean Operations
topics.learn: There are three basic Boolean operations. Every other operation can be made from them. 1. AND operation ( · ) — gives output 1 only when ALL inputs are 1. Expression: Y = A · B (often written just AB). 2. OR operation ( + ) — gives output 1 when ANY input is 1. Expression: Y = A + B. 3. NOT operation ( ' or ¯ ) — inverts (flips) the input. If the input is 1 the output is 0, and if the input is 0 the output is 1. It is a unary operation, meaning it works on only one operand. Expression: Y = A' (also written as A with a bar on top, A̅).

topics.title: 1.1.6 Truth Tables
topics.learn: A truth table shows all possible input combinations and the output for each one, for a logic gate or a circuit. It is the "complete record" of how the circuit behaves. How to create a truth table: Count the number of inputs (n). Calculate total rows = 2n. List all input combinations in binary counting order (0, 1, 2, 3 … in binary). Calculate the output for each combination.

topics.title: 1.1.7 Logic Gates (Basic Gates: AND, OR, NOT)
topics.learn: Logic gates are electronic circuits that perform Boolean operations. They take one or more input bits and produce one output bit. They are the building blocks of all digital systems — a processor contains billions of them. The three basic gates match the three basic operations: the AND gate, the OR gate and the NOT gate (also called an inverter).

topics.title: 1.1.7 Universal Logic Gates (NAND and NOR)
topics.learn: NAND means "NOT AND": it is an AND gate followed by a NOT. NOR means "NOT OR": an OR gate followed by a NOT. On the symbol, the NOT is shown as a small bubble at the output. NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any logic circuit in the world can be built using only NAND gates (or only NOR gates). Factories like this: they can mass-produce one type of chip and build everything from it.

topics.title: 1.1.7 Advanced Logic Gates (XOR and XNOR)
topics.learn: XOR (Exclusive OR) gives output 1 when the inputs are different. Expression: Y = A ⊕ B. In terms of basic operations, A ⊕ B = A'B + AB'. XNOR (Exclusive NOR) is XOR followed by NOT. It gives output 1 when the inputs are the same. Expression: Y = (A ⊕ B)' = A'B' + AB. The XOR symbol is an OR symbol with an extra curved line at the input side. XNOR adds a bubble at the output.

topics.title: 1.1.8 – 1.1.10 Logic Expressions, Minterms and Maxterms
topics.learn: A logic expression (Boolean expression) combines variables with operations, for example Y = A + B'·C. To evaluate it correctly you must follow the order of precedence, just like BODMAS in maths: Sometimes you are given a truth table and must find the expression. There are two standard ways. Minterm (used in SOP — Sum of Products): a product (AND) of all the variables, written for a row whose output is 1. A variable is complemented (A') if its value is 0, and uncomplemented (A) if its value is 1. OR-ing all the minterms gives the SOP expression. Maxterm (used in POS — Product of Sums): a sum (OR) of all the variables, written for a row whose output is 0. A variable is complemented (A') if its value is 1, and uncomplemented (A) if its value is 0. AND-ing all the maxterms gives the POS expression.

topics.title: 1.1.11 Logic Diagrams
topics.learn: A logic diagram shows how logic gates are connected to create a circuit. It is a "picture" of a Boolean expression. To draw one, use the order of precedence: the operation with the highest priority is drawn first (nearest the inputs), and the last operation is the gate that gives the final output.

Common mistake: Do not draw a separate wire for a variable each time it appears and then leave one unconnected. Every gate input must be joined to an input variable or to another gate's output, and every wire should be clearly labelled in exams. Write the precedence steps in one line, draw neat gate symbols with labelled intermediate outputs (like A·B), and finish with the truth table. topics.title: 1.1.13 Karnaugh Maps (K-Maps)
topics.learn: A Karnaugh map (K-map) is a graphical tool used to simplify Boolean expressions. It is a grid of cells — one cell for each row of the truth table. The cells are arranged so that neighbouring (adjacent) cells differ by only ONE bit. This ordering is called Gray code. You write the output (1 or 0) of each row into its cell, then group the 1s in rectangles of size 1, 2, 4 or 8 (powers of 2). Each group becomes one simple term. This simplifies the equation without long algebra. Grouping rules Group only 1s. Groups must be rectangles of size 1, 2, 4 or 8 — never 3, 5 or 6. Make groups as large as possible. Bigger groups give simpler terms. Use as few groups as possible, but every 1 must be in at least one group. Overlapping is allowed — a 1 may be used in more than one group. Wrapping around the edges is allowed: a cell in the far-left column is adjacent to the cell in the far-right column (BC = 00 is next to BC = 10). To read a group: variables that change (0 to 1) inside the group are eliminated. Variables that stay the same are kept — plain if they stay 1, complemented if they stay 0.
topics.urdu: کارنو میپ (K-Map) بولین ایکسپریشن کو آسان بنانے کا تصویری طریقہ ہے۔ اس کے ساتھ والے خانوں میں صرف ایک بِٹ کا فرق ہوتا ہے (گرے کوڈ: 00، 01، 11، 10)۔ 1 والے خانوں کو 1، 2، 4 یا 8 کے گروپوں میں جتنا بڑا ممکن ہو جوڑیں؛ گروپ ایک دوسرے پر چڑھ سکتے ہیں اور کناروں سے گھوم کر بھی بن سکتے ہیں۔ گروپ کے اندر جو متغیر بدلتا ہے وہ ختم ہو جاتا ہے۔

Put 1 in those cells, 0 elsewhere. Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 2: The two 1s are in the same column, one above the other. Make one group of 2. Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3: Inside the group, A changes (0 then 1) → eliminate A. B stays 1 → keep B. Worked example sketchnote 5: Result: Y = B. Worked example sketchnote 7: Step 1: Put 1s in cells 0, 1 and 3. Worked example sketchnote 8: Step 2: Group 1 = the top row (cells 0 and 1). A stays 0, B changes → term A'. Worked example sketchnote 9: Step 3: Group 2 = the right column (cells 1 and 3). A changes, B stays 1 → term B. Cell 1 is used twice — overlapping is allowed. Worked example sketchnote 10: Result: Y = A' + B. Worked example sketchnote 12: Step 1: Fill the map. Careful — the columns are in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10, so m₃ is in the third column and m₂ in the fourth. Worked example sketchnote 13: Step 2: No group of 4 is possible (there is no 2×2 block or full row of 1s). So make groups of 2, each using m₇: Worked example sketchnote 14: Result: Y = AB + BC + AC. Four 3-variable terms (needing 4 three-input AND gates) became three 2-variable terms. Worked example sketchnote 15: Check one row: A=1, B=0, C=1 → AB = 0, BC = 0, AC = 1 → Y = 1. In the truth table, row 5 is 1. ✓ Worked example sketchnote 16: Group 1: m₃ + m₇ (column BC = 11). A changes; B = 1, C = 1 stay → BC. Worked example sketchnote 17: Group 2: m₅ + m₇ (row A = 1, columns 01 and 11). B changes; A = 1, C = 1 stay → AC. Worked example sketchnote 18: Group 3: m₇ + m₆ (row A = 1, columns 11 and 10). C changes; A = 1, B = 1 stay → AB. Worked example sketchnote 19: K-map example 4 (3 variables, wrap-around): simplify Y = Σm(0, 2, 4, 6). Worked example sketchnote 20: Step 1: The 1s are in the far-left column (BC = 00) and the far-right column (BC = 10). Worked example sketchnote 21: Step 2: Because the map wraps around, these two columns are adjacent. Make one group of 4: m₀, m₄, m₂, m₆. Worked example sketchnote 22: Step 3: In this group A changes (0, 1) and B changes (0, 1). Only C stays the same: C = 0 → term C'. Worked example sketchnote 23: Result: Y = C'. Without wrapping you would get two groups (B'C' + BC'), which is correct but not the simplest. Worked example sketchnote 24: K-map example 5 (3 variables): simplify Y = Σm(1, 4, 5, 6, 7) — this is the output of Y = A + B'C from 1.1.8. Worked example sketchnote 25: Step 1: Group of 4: the whole row A = 1 (m₄, m₅, m₇, m₆). B and C both change; A stays 1 → A. Worked example sketchnote 26: Step 2: m₁ is still alone. Pair it with m₅ below it (column BC = 01). A changes; B = 0, C = 1 stay → B'C. Worked example sketchnote 27: Result: Y = A + B'C — the K-map confirms the original expression was already in its simplest form. Worked example sketchnote 28: Going further — a 4-variable K-map: simplify Y = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15). (Not required by the slides, but a good test of the same rules.) 4 variables need 16 cells; both rows (AB) and columns (CD) use Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10. Worked example sketchnote 29: Step 1: The centre 2×2 block (m₅, m₇, m₁₃, m₁₅) is a group of 4. A and C change; B = 1 and D = 1 stay → BD. Worked example sketchnote 30: Step 2: The four corners (m₀, m₂, m₈, m₁₀) are adjacent through wrap-around (left–right and top–bottom). A and C change; B = 0 and D = 0 stay → B'D'. Worked example sketchnote 31: Result: Y = BD + B'D' (this is B XNOR D). Eight 4-variable minterms became two 2-variable terms. Yaad rakhna: Gray code song: "zero-zero, zero-one, one-one, one-zero" — only one bit flips at each step. Imagine the K-map is drawn on a tube, so the left and right edges touch. topics.title: LogiSim Evolution: Simulation Tool
topics.learn: LogiSim Evolution is a free graphical tool for designing and simulating logic circuits. "Simulating" means the computer pretends to be the real circuit: you can switch inputs on and off and watch the output change. It lets you see the truth tables and Boolean expressions you learn in theory.

topics.title: 1.2.1 – 1.2.3 Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
topics.learn: The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured process that guides software development from beginning to end. It ensures clear goals, better planning, risk reduction and high quality. Without it, teams forget features, go over budget and deliver buggy software. SDLC has 6 phases:
topics.urdu: ایس ڈی ایل سی (SDLC) سافٹ ویئر بنانے کا منظم طریقہ ہے جس کے چھ مراحل ہیں: ضروریات کا تجزیہ، سسٹم ڈیزائن، کوڈنگ (Implementation)، ٹیسٹنگ، تنصیب (Deployment) اور دیکھ بھال (Maintenance)۔ پہلا مرحلہ سب سے اہم ہے اور اس سے SRS دستاویز بنتی ہے۔ بلیک باکس ٹیسٹنگ میں کوڈ نظر نہیں آتا جبکہ وائٹ باکس ٹیسٹنگ میں کوڈ دیکھ کر اندرونی منطق جانچی جاتی ہے۔

DeploymentRelease the software to end-users: Direct, Phased, or Pilot release.Live Software 6. MaintenanceProvide support and updates, and fix post-release issues.Patches, Updated Versions Deployment methods: In a direct release the old system is switched off and the new one switched on at once. Worked example sketchnote 2: Phase 1 (Requirements): you ask the family what rooms they need — 3 bedrooms, a kitchen, a garage. Worked example sketchnote 7: Phase 6 (Maintenance): repairs, painting and a new room added later. Worked example sketchnote 8: Black box vs white box on a login screen. A black-box tester types a correct password and a wrong password and checks that the first is accepted and the second rejected — without looking at the code. A white-box tester (the developer) reads the code and checks that every if branch, for example the "account locked after 3 tries" branch, actually runs correctly. Yaad rakhna: Remember the order with "Real Developers Implement, Test, Deploy, Maintain" (R-D-I-T-D-M). Black box = a closed box (you can't see inside). White box = a glass box (you can see inside). Common mistake: Do not say the SDLC ends at deployment. Maintenance is a full phase and often lasts the longest. Also, the SRS is the deliverable of Requirement Analysis, not of Design. topics.title: 1.2.4 The Waterfall Model

topics.title: 1.2.4 The Agile Model
topics.learn: The Agile model is an iterative approach: the software is built in small, repeated cycles called sprints (usually 2–4 weeks long). Each sprint plans, builds and tests a small part of the software, and then shows it to the customer. Customer feedback is gathered continuously and used in the next sprint.

topics.title: 1.2.5 – 1.2.7 Waterfall vs Agile: Comparison and Case Studies
topics.learn: Both models follow the same SDLC phases. The difference is how they move through them: Waterfall goes through each phase once, in a straight line; Agile goes through all phases many times, in small loops.

topics.title: 1.3.1 – 1.3.4 Communication Models and the OSI 7-Layer Model
topics.learn: A communication model explains how data travels from one device to another through a network. Because sending data is complicated, the job is split into layers; each layer does one part of the job and passes the data to the next layer. The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model was developed by ISO (International Organization for Standardization) in 1984. It divides communication into 7 layers. When you send data, it goes down the layers on your device (7 → 1), travels as bits over the cable or air, and goes up the layers on the receiving device (1 → 7).

topics.title: 1.3.5 – 1.3.6 TCP/IP Model vs OSI Model
topics.learn: The OSI model is mainly a reference model used for teaching and design. The TCP/IP model is the practical model used on the real Internet. It condenses the 7 OSI layers into just 4 layers.

topics.title: 2.1 Computational Thinking
topics.learn: Computational Thinking (CT) is a systematic approach to solving problems. "Systematic" means you follow a fixed, organised method instead of guessing. CT involves four activities: CT is not "thinking like a computer". It is thinking in a way that lets you describe a solution so clearly that a computer (or another person) could carry it out. Decomposition — breaking a big problem down into smaller parts. Pattern recognition — identifying things that repeat or follow a rule. Abstraction — hiding (ignoring) details that do not matter. Algorithms — developing clear step-by-step instructions to solve the problem. Did you know? Pseudocode is a human-readable representation of an algorithm using plain English and structured programming keywords. It is the bridge between human logic and machine code. You will study it in detail in section 2.2.2.

topics.title: 2.2 Algorithm
topics.learn: An algorithm is a step-by-step logical procedure used to solve a problem. It is conceptual in nature (it is an idea, a plan) and completely independent of any programming language. The same algorithm can be written later in Python, C++ or Java. A good algorithm has: Input — the data it starts with. Clear steps — each step has only one meaning. A definite end — it must finish after a limited number of steps. Output — the result it produces.

ReusabilityThey can be reused for similar problems, saving time and effort. A sorting algorithm for marks can also sort prices. A program is the algorithm written in a programming language so that a computer can run it. The algorithm itself is only the logic. topics.title: 2.2.2 Algorithm vs Pseudocode
topics.learn: Both algorithms and pseudocode are used in problem-solving, but they serve different purposes in the design phase. The algorithm says what must be done. The pseudocode shows how it could be implemented, using programming-like keywords such as IF, FOR and WHILE, but it still cannot be run on a computer.

topics.title: 2.3.1 Decomposition
topics.learn: Decomposition is a problem-solving technique in which a complex task or system is broken down into smaller, manageable parts. By dividing a big problem into simpler steps, it becomes easier to understand, develop and solve. Each small part is called a sub-task (or sub-problem). You solve each sub-task separately, then join the solutions to solve the whole problem.
topics.urdu: ڈیکمپوزیشن (Decomposition) کا مطلب ہے کسی بڑے اور پیچیدہ مسئلے کو چھوٹے اور آسان حصوں میں تقسیم کرنا۔ مثلاً نئی زبان سیکھنے کو الفاظ، گرامر، زمانے (Tenses) اور جملہ سازی میں تقسیم کیا جا سکتا ہے۔ اس سے پیچیدگی کم ہوتی ہے، غلطی ڈھونڈنا آسان ہوتا ہے اور حصے دوبارہ استعمال ہو سکتے ہیں۔

An algorithmic strategy is a general method that helps you design an algorithm. The three strategies in your syllabus are decomposition, pattern recognition and abstraction. Complex Problem Sub-task 1 Sub-task 2 Sub-task 3 Decomposition: one complex problem is split into smaller sub-tasks. Why is decomposition useful? Reduces complexity: you focus on one piece at a time. Helps in debugging: you can find exactly where the mistake is (e.g., in the language example, is the error in the verb tense or the word order?). Promotes reusability: once you learn or build a small part, you can apply it elsewhere (the "calculate percentage" part can be reused in an attendance program). topics.title: 2.3.2 Pattern Recognition
topics.learn: Pattern recognition is the process of identifying regularities, repetitions or rules in data. It helps in reducing the overall complexity of an algorithm and forms the foundation of concepts such as loops. How it works — ask yourself three questions: What is repeating? What changes in a predictable way? Can I generalise this (write one rule that works for every case)?

topics.title: 2.3.3 Abstraction
topics.learn: Abstraction means hiding unnecessary features and focusing only on the essential ones needed to solve a problem. It reduces complexity by ignoring what is not important (the noise). When you apply abstraction you sort details into three groups: Necessary steps — the core logic that never changes. Changes based on the situation — these become variables (inputs) in the algorithm. Abstraction items (noise) — details you can ignore completely.

topics.title: 2.4.1 Sorting Algorithms: Bubble Sort
topics.learn: Bubble Sort is an elementary sorting algorithm that works by repeatedly comparing adjacent (side-by-side) elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. In each pass, the largest remaining value "bubbles up" to the end of the list, like an air bubble rising to the top of water. So after pass 1 the largest value is in the last place, after pass 2 the second largest is in second-last place, and so on. A list of N items needs N − 1 passes, and pass K makes N − K comparisons.
topics.urdu: ببل سارٹ (Bubble Sort) میں ساتھ ساتھ موجود دو عناصر کا موازنہ کیا جاتا ہے اور اگر وہ غلط ترتیب میں ہوں تو ان کی جگہ بدل دی جاتی ہے۔ ہر پاس (Pass) کے بعد سب سے بڑا عدد آخر میں پہنچ جاتا ہے۔ N عناصر کے لیے N−1 پاس درکار ہوتے ہیں۔ یہ سمجھنے میں آسان اور مستحکم (Stable) ہے لیکن بڑے ڈیٹا کے لیے بہت سست ہے۔

Matlab یہ ہوا کہ In each pass, the largest remaining value "bubbles up" to the end of the list, like an air bubble rising to the top of water. Set temp = DATA[PTR] 2. Set DATA[PTR] = DATA[PTR+1] 3. Set DATA[PTR+1] = temp b: Set PTR := PTR + 1 Step 7: End Pseudocode Start DATA = {8,4,1,9,3} N = 5 For outer = 0 to N-1 For inner = 0 to N-2-outer IF DATA[inner] > DATA[inner+1] Temp = DATA[inner] DATA[inner] = DATA[inner+1] DATA[inner+1] = Temp End If End For End For End Advantages and disadvantages AdvantagesDisadvantages Easiest algorithm to visualise and explain.Uses nested loops, so the time grows very fast as the list grows (about N² comparisons). Does not need extra memory (in-place sorting).Performs a massive number of swaps. Stable (equal items stay in their original order).Useless for real-world "Big Data". Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: sort 8, 4, 1, 9, 3 in ascending order. The pair in brackets [ ] is being compared. Positions are counted from 1. Worked example sketchnote 2: 9 is now at its correct (final) place. Worked example sketchnote 3: Sorted list: 1, 3, 4, 8, 9. Totals: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons and 6 swaps. Worked example sketchnote 4: Bubble Sort in Python (follows the pseudocode exactly; Python indexes start at 0): Worked example sketchnote 5: range(n - 1 - outer) gives inner = 0 … N−2−outer, exactly as in the pseudocode. Notice the list was already sorted after pass 3, but the plain algorithm still does pass 4. Yaad rakhna: Bubble = neighbours. Bubble Sort only ever compares neighbours (j and j+1). topics.title: 2.4.1 Sorting Algorithms: Selection Sort
topics.learn: Selection Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that works by repeatedly selecting the smallest element from the unsorted portion of the list and moving it to its correct position at the front. Think of it as filling seats from the front: first find who belongs in position 1, then position 2, and so on. In the textbook version, the element at position K is compared with every element after it; whenever a smaller one is found, the two are swapped. So at the end of pass K, the K-th smallest value sits in position K.

Performs fewer swaps overall compared to Bubble Sort.Must finish every single loop — it is "blind" to an already sorted list. Does not need extra memory.Not stable (it might change the relative positions of equal items). Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: sort 8, 4, 1, 9, 3 in ascending order (textbook method). topics.learn: Linear Search, also known as sequential search, works by examining each element in the list one by one, from the start, until the target is found (or the list ends). It works on both sorted and unsorted data. A flag variable (here ValueFound) starts at 0 and becomes 1 when the item is found. After the loop, the flag tells us whether to print the item or "Not Found".

topics.title: 2.4.2 Searching Algorithms: Binary Search
topics.learn: Binary Search is a highly efficient search algorithm that works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. Crucial limitation: it only works on a SORTED list. Three variables mark the part of the list still being searched: At each step compare the item with DATA[MID]: If BEG becomes greater than END, the part is empty and the item is not in the list. BEG (low) — first position of the current part. END (high) — last position of the current part. MID = INT((BEG + END) / 2) — the middle position. INT means "drop the decimal part". Equal → found, stop. Item < DATA[MID] → the item can only be in the left half: set END = MID − 1. Item > DATA[MID] → the item can only be in the right half: set BEG = MID + 1.
topics.urdu: بائنری سرچ (Binary Search) ایک تیز رفتار طریقہ ہے جو ہر قدم پر تلاش کے حصے کو آدھا کر دیتا ہے۔ یہ صرف ترتیب شدہ (Sorted) فہرست پر کام کرتا ہے۔ درمیانی عنصر (MID) سے موازنہ کیا جاتا ہے: اگر مطلوبہ چیز چھوٹی ہو تو بائیں آدھے حصے میں، اور بڑی ہو تو دائیں آدھے حصے میں تلاش جاری رہتی ہے۔ دس لاکھ عناصر میں بھی تقریباً بیس قدموں میں نتیجہ مل جاتا ہے۔

Matlab یہ ہوا کہ Item < DATA[MID] → the item can only be in the left half: set END = MID − 1. اگلی بات یہ ہے: Item > DATA[MID] → the item can only be in the right half: set BEG = MID + 1. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: BEG = first, END = last→MID = INT((BEG+END)/2)→Item = DATA[MID]? Found→Item < DATA[MID]: END = MID−1→Else: BEG = MID+1→Repeat while BEG ≤ END Algorithm (textbook summary) Step 1: Start Step 2: DATA := {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9} (Sorted) Step 3: BEG = 1, END = 9 Step 4: MID = INT((BEG+END)/2) Step 5: Item = 7 Step 6: LOC = 0 Step 7: Repeat while BEG <= END AND DATA[MID] != Item Step 8: If Item < DATA[MID]: END = MID - 1 Else: BEG = MID + 1 Step 9: MID = INT((BEG+END)/2) Step 10: [End loop] Step 11: If DATA[MID] == Item: LOC = MID Else: LOC = 0 Step 12: Print result based on LOC Step 13: End Pseudocode Start DATA = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9} BEG = 1, END = 9 MID = INT((BEG+END)/2) Item = 7 LOC = NULL While BEG <= END AND DATA[MID] != Item IF Item < DATA[MID] then END = MID - 1 Else BEG = MID + 1 End If MID = INT((BEG+END)/2) End While If DATA[MID] == Item then LOC = MID Else LOC = NULL End If If LOC != NULL then Print DATA[MID] Else Print "Not Found" End If End Why is it so fast? Every comparison throws away half of the remaining list. 1,000,000 → 500,000 → 250,000 → … → 1 takes about 20 halvings, because \(2^{20}\) = 1,048,576. So Binary Search finds an item among 1 million elements in at most ab Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example 1 (textbook algorithm). DATA = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; Item = 7. Positions 1 to 9. Worked example sketchnote 2: Only 2 comparisons. Linear Search would need 7. Worked example sketchnote 3: Worked example 2 (slide example). Sorted list: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Searching item: 3. Worked example sketchnote 4: Picture the list shrinking (the highlighted cell is MID): Worked example sketchnote 5: The slide describes the same steps using the size of each sub-list: Step 1 MID = 8/2 = 4 (value 4), 3 < 4, go left; Step 2 sub-list [1, 2, 3], middle = 3/2 = 1.5 → 2nd item (value 2), 3 > 2, go right; Step 3 sub-list [3], middle = 1st item (value 3), FOUND. Both ways land on the same values 4 → 2 → 3. Worked example sketchnote 6: Binary Search in Python (index starts at 0, so positions 1–8 become indexes 0–7): Worked example sketchnote 7: // is integer division, the same as INT(). Index 2 is position 3. Here loc = -1 means "not found", so the test loc >= 0 is correct. Yaad rakhna: Binary Search is how you find a word in a dictionary: open the middle, decide "before or after?", and throw away half the book each time. "Sorted first, then split." Common mistake: The slide's pseudocode writes the loop condition as BEG <= END OR DATA[MID] != Item. That is a slip: with OR the loop would never stop once the item is found while BEG ≤ END. The textbook algorithm (Step 7) correctly uses AND — keep going only while the part is not empty and the item is not yet found. Likewise, the slide sets LOC = NULL but then tests "LOC >= 0"; the check should simply be "LOC is not NULL" (or, with LOC = 0 meaning not found, "LOC > 0"). The pseudocode above shows the corrected form. Common errors: (1) using Binary Search on an unsorted list — the answer will be wrong; (2) setting END = MID instead of MID − 1 (or BEG = MID instead of MID + 1), which can cause an infinite loop — this is the "off-by-one" error; (3) forgetting INT, so MID becomes a decimal like 4.5. topics.title: 2.5 Evaluation Criteria of Algorithm
topics.learn: Many algorithms can solve the same problem. To judge which is better, we evaluate them on three criteria: correctness, efficiency and clarity.
topics.urdu: کسی الگورتھم کو تین معیارات پر پرکھا جاتا ہے: درستگی (Correctness) یعنی درست نتیجہ دے، غیر معمولی صورتوں کو سنبھالے اور ہمیشہ ختم ہو؛ کارکردگی (Efficiency) یعنی کم وقت اور کم میموری استعمال کرے؛ اور وضاحت (Clarity) یعنی پڑھنے، سمجھنے اور تبدیل کرنے میں آسان ہو۔ درستگی جانچنے کے لیے ٹریس ٹیبل (Trace Table) بنایا جاتا ہے۔

To judge which is better, we evaluate them on three criteria: correctness, efficiency and clarity. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: 2.5.1 Correctness An algorithm is correct if: its output matches the expected outcomes; it handles edge cases gracefully (unusual inputs such as an empty list, 0, a negative number, or an item that is not present); it is guaranteed to finish — no infinite loops. We test correctness with a trace table (dry run): we feed sample inputs and record every value by hand, then compare the result with what we expect. 2.5.2 Efficiency We measure algorithm efficiency through time (speed) and space (memory). The key question is: how fast does it run as the input size grows — does it scale well? Computer scientists describe growth with Big O notation. It counts roughly how many steps are needed for N items: \(O(1)\) — constant: same time, whatever N is. O(log N) — logarithmic: grows very slowly (Binary Search). O(N) — linear: double N, double the time (Linear Search). \(O(N^{2})\) — quadratic: double N, four times the time (Bubble and Selection Sort). 2.5.3 Clarity (Readability) An algorithm must be easy to read, understand and modify. It should use clear steps, meaningful variable names and good indentation. Unclear a=[3,6,15] for x in a: if x%2==0:print(x,"E") else:print(x,"O") Clear numbers  Worked example sketchnote 1: Trace table example: Even/Odd checker. Rule: divide the number by 2; if the remainder is 0 it is Even, otherwise Odd. Worked example sketchnote 2: All three results match what we expect, so the algorithm is correct for these inputs. The same check in Python: Worked example sketchnote 3: A good tester would also try the edge case 0 (remainder 0 → Even, which is correct). Worked example sketchnote 4: How the worst-case number of comparisons grows Worked example sketchnote 5: This is why Binary Search is called excellent for Big Data and the simple sorts are called useless for it. Yaad rakhna: Remember C-E-C: Correct (right answer, always finishes), Efficient (fast and light), Clear (easy to read). Common mistake: Testing only "normal" inputs is not enough to prove correctness. Always include edge cases in your trace table, e.g., the first item, the last item, a missing item, or an empty list in a search. topics.title: 2.6 How to Decide Which Algorithm to Use
topics.learn: Before choosing an algorithm, ask three questions: Simple decision guide: What is the input size? (10 items or 10 million?) Is the data sorted? Do we need speed or memory efficiency? If searching on unsorted data → use Linear Search. If searching on sorted data → use Binary Search. If data needs ordering → use a sorting algorithm.

topics.title: 3.1 Programming
topics.learn: Computers are "dumb" machines. They are very fast, but they cannot think or do anything on their own. They need exact, step-by-step instructions. A set of instructions given to a computer is called a program. The language used to write these instructions is called a programming language. Writing programs is called programming, and the person who writes them is a programmer.

topics.title: 3.1.1 Programming Language Types
topics.learn: Programming languages are classified into three main types, depending on how close they are to the computer's own language (binary 0s and 1s) or to human language.

topics.title: 3.2 Career Growth with Python
topics.learn: Python is one of the most in-demand languages in the world. Learning it opens many career paths: Software Development: build desktop and web applications. Data Science and Data Analysis: analyse data, create reports and make predictions. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: develop intelligent systems, chatbots and recommendation algorithms (like "videos you may like"). Web Development: use frameworks such as Django and Flask to build websites. Automation and Scripting: automate repetitive office or lab tasks (renaming 500 files, filling spreadsheets). Cybersecurity and Networking: write security tools and analyse network data.

topics.title: 3.3 Integrated Development Environment (IDE)
topics.learn: An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is a software tool that helps programmers write, run and manage code in one place. It is a complete workspace for programming. "Integrated" means many tools are joined together in one window. Key features of an IDE: Code Editor: where you write and edit code. Syntax Highlighting: colours different parts of the code (keywords, strings, numbers) to make it easier to read. Auto-completion: suggests code while you type (type pri and it offers print). Run/Execute Tool: runs the program with one click. Debugger: helps you find and fix errors, for example by pausing the program at a chosen line.

topics.title: 3.4 Fundamentals of Python Programming
topics.learn: The basic structure of a Python program is simple and clear. A program takes data, processes it using statements, and finally shows output. Python runs the statements top to bottom, one after another (sequentially). A statement is one complete instruction, usually written on one line, such as print("Hi") or x = 5. 1. Comments (#) — Comments are notes written in the code for humans. They start with the # symbol. The Python interpreter completely ignores them. Use them to explain what your code does. 2. Indentation (spaces) — C++ and Java use curly brackets { } to mark a block of code (a group of statements that belong together). Python instead uses indentation: spaces at the beginning of a line. Indentation is mandatory in Python. The standard is 4 spaces (or 1 tab).

topics.title: 3.4.1 Variables
topics.learn: A variable is a named space in computer memory used to store data. Think of it as a labelled container (a box with a name written on it). You put a value in it with the assignment operator =, which means "store", not "equals". In Python you do not need to declare the type of a variable. Python figures it out automatically from the value. This is called dynamic typing: the same variable can later hold a different type. Rules for naming variables: Can contain letters, numbers and underscores (_) only — no spaces or symbols like -, @, $. Must start with a letter or underscore, NOT a number (1name is invalid). Are case-sensitive: age and Age are two completely different variables. Cannot be a Python keyword (a reserved word such as if, for, while, else, True).

topics.title: 3.4.2 Input and Output Handling
topics.learn: Output — the print() function. A function is a named, ready-made piece of code that does a job when you call it with brackets. print() displays information on the screen. Input — the input() function. It shows a message (a prompt), pauses the program and waits for the user to type something and press Enter. Whatever the user types is always a string by default. Type casting means converting a value from one type to another: int() converts to an integer, float() to a decimal number, str() to a string. Items separated by commas are printed with one space between them. An f-string (a string with f before the quote) lets you put variables directly inside { }. It is the fastest and most readable way to format output.

topics.learn: An operand is the value or variable being worked on. An operator is the symbol that performs the action. Together they form an expression, which Python evaluates to a single value. In 10 + 20: 10 is an operand, + is the operator, 20 is an operand, and the result is 30. 1. Arithmetic operators do maths:

Order of operations (precedence). Python follows the same order as maths (like BODMAS): brackets first, then **, then * / // % (left to right), then + - (left to right). ** is the exception: it works right to left. print(2 + 3 * 4) print((2 + 3) * 4) print(2 ** 3 ** 2) print(10 - 4 - 3) print(-9 // 2) print(17 % 5, 17 // 5) 14 20 512 3 -5 2 3 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 2 ** 9 = 512 (right to left). -9 // 2 is -5 because floor division always rounds down to the smaller whole number (−4.5 → −5). 2. Assignment operators store a value in a variable, often updating it. The short forms are called compound assignment. topics.title: 3.4.3 Bitwise Operators
topics.learn: 6. Bitwise operators treat numbers as binary digits (bits: 0s and 1s) and work on them bit by bit, column by column. Think of each bit as a switch that is ON (1) or OFF (0). Python's bin() function shows the binary form of a number (it starts with 0b). AND (&) — gives 1 only if both bits are 1, otherwise 0. OR (|) — gives 1 if at least one bit is 1. XOR (^) — gives 1 if the bits are different, 0 if they are the same. NOT (~) — inverts all bits (0 → 1, 1 → 0). In Python the result is the number made negative, minus 1: ~x = -(x + 1). So ~10 gives -11. Left shift (<<) — moves bits left and adds 0s on the right. Each shift multiplies by 2. Right shift (>>) — moves bits right and removes the rightmost bits. Each shift divides by 2 (floor division).

topics.title: 3.5 Control Structures
topics.learn: Control structures decide the order in which statements are executed in a program (the "flow of control"). Almost every program is built from just three basic structures: Sequence — do the steps one after another, top to bottom. Selection — choose a path depending on a condition (if, else). Repetition — repeat steps (loops: for, while).

topics.title: 3.5.2 Selection Statements: if and if-else
topics.learn: Selection changes the flow of a program based on a condition — an expression that is either True or False. It helps a program respond intelligently to different situations. 1. The if statement executes a block of code only if the condition is True. If the condition is False, the block is completely skipped. 2. The if-else statement provides two paths: if the condition is true, do this; else (otherwise), do that. Exactly one of the two blocks always runs.

topics.title: 3.5.2 Selection Statements: if-elif-else and Nested if

As soon as it finds a True condition, it runs that block and ignores all the rest. If none is True, the else block runs. 4. Nested if is an if inside another if. topics.title: 3.5.3 The while Loop, break and continue
topics.learn: 2. The while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition remains True. It is used when the exact number of iterations is not known in advance (for example, "keep asking until the password is correct"). A while loop needs three parts: (1) initialise a variable before the loop, (2) test the condition, (3) update the variable inside the loop. If you forget the update, the condition never becomes False and the loop never stops — an infinite loop. Loop control statements change the normal flow of a loop: break — exits (stops) the loop entirely and immediately. continue — skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one.

topics.title: 3.5.3 Nested Loops and for vs while
topics.learn: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely, from start to finish, for every single iteration of the outer loop. If the outer loop runs 2 times and the inner loop runs 3 times, the inner body runs 2 × 3 = 6 times.

topics.title: Practical Activity: Shopping Bill Calculator
topics.learn: This program combines all three control structures: sequence (steps in order), selection (checking "done", checking the price, checking for a discount) and repetition (a while loop that keeps adding items). It uses a flag — a Boolean variable (shopping) that controls when the loop stops. item.lower() converts the text to lowercase so that "done", "Done" and "DONE" all work.

topics.title: 3.6 Libraries in Python
topics.learn: A library (also called a module) is a collection of pre-written code that offers ready-made functions. Instead of writing a square-root algorithm from scratch, you import math and call math.sqrt(). Libraries save time, reduce bugs and let you stand on other programmers' work. There are five common ways to import a library. Method 3 (import only what you need) is the best habit: it is clearer and uses less memory than from math import *.

topics.title: 4.1.1 Data, Information and Database
topics.learn: Data are unprocessed facts, figures or observations. They can be quantitative (numbers: 80, 75, 90) or qualitative (descriptions: the colours of cars in a parking lot). Data on its own is not very useful — a list of marks does not yet tell you whether the class is strong. When you organise, process and interpret data, it becomes information. Information has meaning and supports a decision. Example: “The class average is 80%, so we can move to the next chapter.” A database is an organised collection of related data, stored in a structured way so it can be accessed, managed and updated easily. Paper registers and loose files make searching painful; a database is built for search, update and sharing.

topics.title: 4.1.2 Database Management System (DBMS)
topics.learn: A DBMS is software that lets you create, manage and interact with databases. It sits between the user and the stored files. You never edit raw data files by hand — you talk to the DBMS (Access, MySQL, Oracle, SQLite) and it handles storage, security and consistency. Advantages you must be able to list: Less redundancy. The department name is stored once, not in every student row. Consistency. Change a phone number once; every screen that uses it shows the new number. Security. Only authorised users see sensitive fields (an admin sees marks; office staff see names). Integrity. Rules stop duplicate roll numbers and empty primary keys.

topics.title: 4.2 Database Components (Tables, Records, Fields)
topics.learn: The basic structure is a table (also called a relation): rows and columns, like a spreadsheet, holding facts about one kind of thing (Students, Teachers, Books). A record (row, tuple) is one complete instance — everything about Ali. A field (column, attribute) is one kind of fact — the whole Name column, or the whole Grade column.

topics.title: 4.3.1 Keys and Integrity Constraints
topics.learn: A key is a field (or a set of fields) that uniquely identifies records and links tables. Integrity constraints are the rules that keep those keys honest. Candidate key. Any field (or combination) that could uniquely identify a row. A table may have several. In an Employee table: EmpID, EmpLicense# and EmpPassport are all candidate keys. Primary key (PK). The one candidate you actually choose. Rules: unique, never NULL, only one PK per table (it may be a composite of two columns). Example: EmpID. Alternate key. The leftover candidate keys. After EmpID is chosen, EmpLicense# and EmpPassport become alternate keys — still unique, just not “the” identifier. Foreign key (FK). A field in this table that refers to the PK of another table. It may contain duplicates (many employees in one department) and, in some designs, NULL.

topics.title: 4.3 Relational Database Management System (RDBMS)
topics.learn: An RDBMS stores data in several tables and uses primary and foreign keys to keep relationships. Banks, universities and NADRA use RDBMS software. Extra strengths on top of a plain DBMS: Reduces redundancy by splitting data into related tables. Supports many users at once, with permissions. Is queried with SQL (Structured Query Language) — a standard language of SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.

topics.title: 4.5 Referential Integrity
topics.learn: Referential integrity means every foreign-key value in a child table must match an existing primary-key value in the parent — or be NULL if the design allows it. It stops orphan records. If Result.StudentID is a FK to Student.StudentID, you cannot type Result for student 999 if 999 is not in Student. You also cannot delete student 101 while results for 101 still exist — unless you first handle those child rows.

topics.title: 4.6 Relational Schema Development
topics.learn: A relational schema is the formal written design of the database: table names, fields, primary keys, foreign keys and how tables relate. You write it before clicking around in Access. It defines (1) how data is split into tables, (2) which columns each table has, (3) which fields are PK/FK, (4) the relationships. Benefits: less redundancy, integrity planned in advance, easier to grow later.

topics.title: 4.7 Case Study — Library Management System
topics.learn: A college library needs a database. Walk the seven steps examiners expect. Step 1 — Requirements. A book has ID, title, author, publisher. A member (student/teacher) has ID, name, contact. A member can borrow many books; a book can be borrowed by different members over time. Record Issue Date and Return Date. Step 2 — Entities. Book, Member. (Borrowing will need a third entity in step 6.) Step 3 — Attributes. Book: BookID (PK), Title, Author, Publisher. Member: MemberID (PK), Name, ContactInfo. Step 4 — Relationship. Member borrows Book. Step 5 — Cardinality. One member borrows many books over time; one book is borrowed by many members over time → M:N. Step 6 — Resolve M:N. Add junction entity BorrowRecord: BorrowID (PK), MemberID (FK), BookID (FK), IssueDate, ReturnDate. Now Member 1—M BorrowRecord M—1 Book (two 1:M links). Step 7 — Final schema.

A form with no source has nowhere to save. Form Wizard (the exam method): Create tab → Form Wizard. Select the table (e.g. Student). Move fields with > (one) or >> (all). Choose layout. Columnar = one record at a time, best for data entry. Name it (“Student Registration”) → Finish.

topics.title: 5.1 Introduction to Computing Impacts
topics.learn: Computing means using computers and computer-based devices to store, process and share information. Today computing is an important part of your daily life. You use computers, mobile phones, the internet and smart devices almost everywhere — at home, in college and on the road. In Pakistan, computing is becoming vital (very necessary) in: An impact is the effect something has on people and society. Computing has positive impacts (speed, convenience, new jobs) and negative impacts (privacy risks, addiction, job loss). In this chapter you will study three key technologies first — AI, IoT and Data Analytics — and then their uses and impacts. Schools and colleges — online admissions, e-books, online results of the Sindh boards. Hospitals — computerised patient records, digital X-rays, online appointment systems. Banks — ATMs, mobile banking apps, Raast instant payments, JazzCash and Easypaisa wallets. Farms — weather forecasts on mobile phones, soil sensors, tube-well control. Industries — automatic machines in textile mills in Karachi, Hyderabad and Faisalabad.

topics.title: 5.1.1 Artificial Intelligence (AI)
topics.learn: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human thinking, such as recognising faces, understanding language and making decisions. Understand the name in two parts: AI systems use data to make decisions. The more good data an AI system sees, the better it becomes at recognising patterns (repeating features) and predicting what to do. Examples from the source: More Pakistani examples: Google Maps predicting traffic on Shahrah-e-Faisal, Urdu voice typing on your phone, banks flagging a suspicious card transaction, and AI tools that translate English into Urdu. Artificial — it is created by humans; it is not natural. Intelligence — it can perform tasks that require thinking. Face recognition on a mobile phone to unlock the screen. YouTube suggesting videos based on your interests. Chatbots answering questions on a website (for example, a bank's help chat).

Example سے سمجھو: Examples from the source: یاد رکھنا: More Pakistani examples: Google Maps predicting traffic on Shahrah-e-Faisal, Urdu voice typing on your phone, banks flagging a suspicious card transaction, and AI tools that translate English into Urdu. ایک اور point: Artificial — it is created by humans; it is not natural. Matlab یہ ہوا کہ YouTube suggesting videos based on your interests. اگلی بات یہ ہے: Chatbots answering questions on a website (for example, a bank's help chat). Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: AI in smart systems AI rarely works alone. It often acts as the "brain" of a system, working together with the Internet of Things (IoT) and Data Analytics: IoT devices gather data — they are the "eyes" (sensors). Analytics sorts the data — it organises and studies it. AI makes the final decision — it is the "brain". An action follows — something happens in the real world. IoT (Eyes) — collects data→Analytics — sorts data→AI (Brain) — decides→Action Worked example sketchnote 1: Smart air-conditioner in a hot Hyderabad room — trace the system: Worked example sketchnote 2: Step 1 (IoT – eyes). A temperature sensor reads the room temperature: 36 °C. Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 2 (Analytics). The readings of the last 10 minutes are organised: 34, 35, 35, 36 °C — the room is getting hotter. Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3 (AI – brain). The AI compares this with the comfortable limit (say 26 °C) and with the fact that a person is in the room (motion sensor). Decision: "Turn the AC on." Worked example sketchnote 5: Step 4 (Action). A switch turns the AC on automatically. Worked example sketchnote 6: No human pressed a button — the system sensed, thought and acted. Yaad rakhna: Eyes – Sort – Brain – Do. IoT is the eyes, Analytics sorts, AI is the brain, and the actuator does the action. Think of a cricket fielder: his eyes see the ball (IoT), he judges speed and direction (analytics), decides to dive (AI), and his body moves (action). Common mistake: Mistake: "AI means robots." Fix: Most AI is just software — YouTube suggestions, spam filters and face unlock have no robot body. A robot may use AI, but AI itself is the thinking software. topics.title: 5.1.2 Internet of Things (IoT) & Components
topics.learn: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system in which physical devices are connected to the Internet and can collect and share data to perform tasks automatically. The "things" are ordinary objects — watches, cameras, cars, fans, water pumps — that have been given sensors and an internet connection so they can "talk" to each other and to us. Source example: A smartwatch collects your heart-rate data and sends it to your mobile phone, where it is displayed.

Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: Components of IoT systems IoT relies on six foundational components to work properly. #ComponentWhat it doesExamples 1SensorsDevices that collect information from the physical world. They are the "eyes and ears" of the system.Temperature sensor, motion sensor, fingerprint sensor, smoke sensor, soil moisture sensor 2ActuatorsDevices that perform physical actions in response to system commands. They convert digital signals into physical movement.Electric motor, switch, automatic door opener, water valve, fan controller 3ConnectivityThe connection that allows devices to send and receive data. Without it, sensors can't talk to the system.Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, ZigBee, 4G/5G 4Data ProcessingChanging raw data into useful information. Steps: collecting, organising, analysing and deciding.Checking if the room temperature is too hot to trigger the AC 5Cloud ComputingStoring data and using services over the internet instead of local hard drives. Handles massive IoT data.Google Drive, iCloud, online LMS 6User Interface (UI)The component that enables interaction between the user and the device. Helps users see information and give commands.Mobile apps, touch screens, voice commands Understanding ea Worked example sketchnote 1: Smart fire alarm in a Karachi factory — identify all six components: Worked example sketchnote 2: Step 1 — Sensor: A smoke sensor detects smoke near the machines. Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 2 — Connectivity: It sends the reading over the factory Wi-Fi. Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3 — Cloud computing: The reading is stored on an online server along with the history of all sensors. Worked example sketchnote 5: Step 4 — Data processing: The software checks: "Is the smoke level above the safe limit?" Yes → decide "Fire risk!" Worked example sketchnote 6: Step 5 — Actuator: Water valves of the sprinklers open and the alarm bell switch turns on. Worked example sketchnote 7: Step 6 — User interface: The manager's mobile app shows a red alert: "Smoke detected – Hall 3". Yaad rakhna: Sensor senses, Actuator acts. Common mistake: Mistake: Calling a fan controller or water valve a "sensor". Fix: Ask "does it measure something or do something?" A valve opens and closes — it does, so it is an actuator. A soil moisture sensor only measures, so it is a sensor. topics.title: 5.1.3 Data Analytics & Components
topics.learn: Data Analytics is the process of collecting, organising, cleaning, studying and presenting data to find useful information. It helps people make better decisions. Data means raw facts and figures (for example, "72, 45, 88"). Information is data that has been processed so it has meaning ("Ali scored 72%; he passed"). Data Analytics is the bridge from data to information. Source example: A college collects exam marks, calculates percentages, and identifies which students need extra help. This entire process is Data Analytics.

It helps people make better decisions. Matlab یہ ہوا کہ Data means raw facts and figures (for example, "72, 45, 88"). Information is data that has been processed so it has meaning ("Ali scored 72%; he passed"). Data Analytics is the bridge from data to information. اگلی بات یہ ہے: Source example: A college collects exam marks, calculates percentages, and identifies which students need extra help. This entire process is Data Analytics. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: Components of Data Analytics Data Analytics comprises five key components, which happen in order like a pipeline: 1. Collection→2. Storage→3. Cleaning→4. Analysis→5. Visualization Data Collection — Gathering raw information from multiple sources: websites, surveys, sensors, hospital records, bank transactions. Data Storage — Storing data safely and properly after collection. It can be stored in files, databases, spreadsheets or the cloud. Data Cleaning — Identifying and correcting errors in data. Raw data may contain: Duplication of records (the same student entered twice), Incorrect values (typos, e.g. marks "870" instead of "87"), Missing files or records (a student's marks not entered), Improper formats (dates written as 05/10/2026 in one place and "5 Oct 26" in another). Data Analysis — Studying the clean data to identify patterns, trends and relevant information for problem-solving (e.g. finding out which subjects students failed the most). Data Visualization — Creating visual representations of data (plots, charts, graphs) to provide valuable insights at a glance (e.g. a pie chart showing pass vs fail percentage). Worked example sketchnote 1: A college in Sukkur analyses Physics test results (out of 50) for 6 students. Worked example sketchnote 2: Step 1 — Collection: Marks are gathered from the teacher's register. Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 2 — Storage: The marks are typed into a spreadsheet saved on Google Drive (cloud). Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3 — Cleaning: Hina's record is a duplicate → delete one copy. Kashif's 250 is an incorrect value (more than 50) → the register shows 25, so correct it. Sana's marks are missing → ask the teacher; she was absent, so mark her "absent". Worked example sketchnote 5: Step 4 — Analysis: Clean marks: 42, 18, 35, 25. Pass mark is 17 (33% of 50 = 16.5, rounded up). All 4 passed. Percentages: Ayesha 84%, Bilal 36%, Hina 70%, Kashif 50%. Average = (42 + 18 + 35 + 25) ÷ 4 = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 marks = 60%. Bilal is closest to failing → needs extra help. Worked example sketchnote 6: Step 5 — Visualization: A bar chart shows each student's percentage; Bilal's short bar makes the problem visible at a glance. Yaad rakhna: "Cows Sit Calmly And Vote" — Collection, Storage, Cleaning, Analysis, Visualization. Or think of cooking daal: buy the lentils (collect), keep them in a jar (store), pick out stones (clean), cook (analyse), serve beautifully on a plate (visualise). Common mistake: Mistake: Skipping cleaning and going straight to analysis. Fix: Dirty data gives wrong answers. In the example, Kashif's wrong "250" would have made the average (42 + 18 + 35 + 250) ÷ 4 = 86.25 — more than 50, which is impossible. Always clean first. topics.title: 5.2 Uses of IoT in Different Areas
topics.learn: IoT improves efficiency (doing more with less effort), saves time, and enhances the overall quality of life. It plays a significant role in developing modern infrastructure (the basic systems of a country — roads, power, water, hospitals). The source lists six areas.

Parking: Sensors guide drivers to empty parking spaces, e.g. in a large shopping mall car park. Waste management: Smart bins send alerts when full, so trucks collect only full bins instead of driving to every bin. 2. Industrial Automation Sensors check machine temperature and vibration to prevent breakdowns (called predictive maintenance). Automated machines perform repeated tasks precisely. Quality-control sensors check products during manufacturing — for example, in the textile industries of Sindh, cameras and sensors spot faults in cloth as it is woven. 3. Healthcare (Smart Health) Smartwatches continuously measure heart rate and vital signs (pulse, oxygen level). Remote monitoring devices send patient data directly to doctors — vital for rural areas of Pakistan, where a specialist may be hundreds of kilometres away (e.g. a heart patient in Tharparkar monitored by a doctor in Karachi). topics.title: 5.2.1 Scope of AI in Education in Pakistan
topics.learn: Artificial Intelligence is gradually becoming an important part of Pakistan's education system, improving teaching, learning and administration (managing the school: admissions, records, timetables). Practical uses: Benefits: Major challenges in Pakistan: Learning Management Systems (LMS) — online platforms (e.g. Google Classroom, Moodle) where teachers post lessons and assignments; AI features can recommend lessons to each student. Automated grading and digital testing — MCQ tests marked instantly by computer. AI-based career counselling — software that studies a student's marks and interests and suggests suitable fields. Helps students learn at their own speed. Identifies students who need extra help. Supports students with disabilities (Assistive AI), e.g. text-to-speech for a visually impaired student. Limited internet access in rural areas. Lack of computers and digital devices for all students. Need for proper teacher training to use AI tools. Data privacy and security issues — students' personal data must be protected.

topics.title: 5.2.2 Career Connection in IoT and AI
topics.learn: Learning computing skills opens doors to many employers in Pakistan: software houses (e.g. in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad technology parks), telecom companies (Jazz, Telenor), banks, and government IT departments (e.g. NADRA, provincial IT boards). Key skills needed: IoT Engineer: designs smart systems and connected devices (e.g. a smart irrigation kit). Data Analyst: analyses the data generated by IoT systems and produces reports. Programming — Python, C++. Networking — Wi-Fi, protocols (rules for how devices communicate). Electronics — sensors and circuits. Problem-solving.

topics.title: 5.3 Information Sources (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary)
topics.learn: Information sources are ways to find knowledge and data. The internet has vast information, but not all of it is accurate. Sources are divided into three main categories. 1. Primary sources give original, firsthand information straight from people, events or official records. They are highly authentic (genuine).Examples: interviews, photographs, diaries, NADRA official records. 2. Secondary sources contain information that has already been collected and explained by someone else. They summarise or analyse primary data.Examples: textbooks, news reports, research papers, Pakistan Bureau of Statistics reports. 3. Tertiary sources provide highly summarised and organised information derived from both primary and secondary sources. They are used for quick reference.Examples: encyclopedias, Wikipedia, dictionaries, handbooks.
topics.urdu: معلومات کے ذرائع علم اور ڈیٹا تلاش کرنے کے طریقے ہیں، جنہیں تین اقسام میں تقسیم کیا جاتا ہے۔ پرائمری ذرائع براہِ راست اور اصل معلومات دیتے ہیں (جیسے انٹرویو، تصاویر، نادرا کا ریکارڈ)۔ سیکنڈری ذرائع وہ ہیں جن میں کسی اور نے پرائمری معلومات کی وضاحت یا تجزیہ کیا ہو (جیسے درسی کتابیں، خبریں)۔ ٹرشیری ذرائع خلاصہ شدہ معلومات دیتے ہیں جیسے انسائیکلوپیڈیا، وکی پیڈیا اور لغت۔ جس آن لائن مضمون میں مصنف کا نام، تاریخ یا حوالہ جات نہ ہوں اس پر بھروسہ نہ کریں۔

Many examples, sorted Primary (firsthand)Secondary (explained by others)Tertiary (summarised, quick reference) Interview with a flood victim in DaduNewspaper report on the 2022 floodsEncyclopedia entry "Floods in Pakistan" Photograph taken at an eventTextbook chapter explaining the eventWikipedia article Personal diary or letterBiography written by a historianDictionary NADRA official records (CNIC data)Pakistan Bureau of Statistics report analysing census dataHandbook / almanac of facts Original survey responsesResearch paper analysing the surveyIndex or list of research papers Sensor readings from an IoT weather stationTV news analysis of the weatherA school "fact sheet" on climate Quaid-e-Azam's original speech recordingArticle discussing the speechEncyclopedia summary of his life When do sources become unreliable? Written by a person who lived through the event → firsthand → Primary. Worked example sketchnote 3: (b) A Dawn newspaper article analysing the budget. A journalist collected facts and explained them → Secondary. Worked example sketchnote 4: (c) An Oxford English–Urdu dictionary. Organised, summarised reference built from many sources → Tertiary. Worked example sketchnote 5: (d) A Bureau of Statistics report on literacy in Sindh. It analyses census (primary) data → Secondary. topics.title: 5.4 Impacts of Computing in Various Fields
topics.learn: Computing has drastically changed society. It makes life faster and more connected, but it also brings challenges like privacy risks and technology addiction. For every field, think of both sides.
topics.urdu: کمپیوٹنگ نے معاشرے کو بہت بدل دیا ہے۔ تعلیم، مواصلات، کاروبار، صحت اور زراعت میں اس نے کام تیز اور آسان بنائے ہیں، لیکن اس کے ساتھ اسکرین کی لت، سماجی تنہائی، ملازمتوں کا خاتمہ، ہیکنگ اور پرائیویسی کے خطرات بھی پیدا ہوئے ہیں۔ ذمہ دارانہ استعمال کے لیے مضبوط پاس ورڈ رکھیں، جعلی خبریں نہ پھیلائیں، اور کھیل کود کے ساتھ اسکرین ٹائم میں توازن رکھیں۔

It makes life faster and more connected, but it also brings challenges like privacy risks and technology addiction. For every field, think of both sides. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: FieldPositive impact (+)Negative impact (−) EducationOnline classes, e-books and learning apps make studying highly flexible and accessible.Excessive screen time reduces attention spans and causes physical health issues (eye strain, back pain). CommunicationEmails and video calls allow instant, global communication at almost zero cost (e.g. a WhatsApp video call to a relative in Dubai).People interact less in person, leading to social isolation and reduced face-to-face skills. BusinessOnline shopping, digital banking and automation dramatically improve speed and efficiency.Traditional manual jobs are lost to machines; risk of severe cyber-attacks on banks. HealthcareDigital patient records and telemedicine allow doctors to treat remote patients accurately.Patient data privacy is at risk if hospital servers are hacked. AgricultureSmart irrigation and weather forecasting massively increase crop yields.Poor internet access in rural areas means many farmers cannot use these tools. Smart and responsible use Protect personal information and use strong passwords (long, with letters, numbers and symbols; never share your OTP or CNIC details with callers). Do not share fake news or unverifi Worked example sketchnote 1: Scenario analysis — a bank in Karachi moves to mobile banking: Worked example sketchnote 2: Step 1 — Identify the field: Business (banking). Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 2 — Positive: Customers transfer money in seconds from home; no queue at the branch; the bank processes more transactions with fewer staff (speed and efficiency). Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3 — Negative: Some cashier jobs are no longer needed (job loss); hackers may attempt cyber-attacks or phishing SMS to steal accounts. Worked example sketchnote 5: Step 4 — Responsible use: Customers should use strong passwords, never share OTPs, and report suspicious messages. Yaad rakhna: For the five fields, remember "E-C-B-H-A" — Education, Communication, Business, Healthcare, Agriculture — and always write one + and one − for each. Common mistake: Mistake: Writing only positive impacts in a "discuss the impacts" question. Fix: "Impact" means both sides. Examiners expect a balanced answer: advantages, disadvantages, and how to use technology responsibly. topics.title: 5.5 Assistive Technologies
topics.learn: Assistive technologies are devices, software and systems that help people with disabilities or functional limitations (difficulty in seeing, hearing, moving, speaking, remembering, etc.). They allow more people to participate equally in school, work and society. There are four categories:
topics.urdu: معاون ٹیکنالوجیز (Assistive Technologies) وہ آلات، سافٹ ویئر اور نظام ہیں جو معذور افراد کی مدد کرتے ہیں تاکہ وہ اسکول، کام اور معاشرے میں برابر حصہ لے سکیں۔ ان کی چار اقسام ہیں: نقل و حرکت میں مدد (اسمارٹ وہیل چیئر)، حسی مدد (سماعتی آلہ، اسکرین ریڈر، بریل ڈسپلے)، گفتگو میں مدد (اسپیچ جنریٹنگ ڈیوائس) اور ذہنی و تعلیمی مدد (آڈیو بکس، اسپیل چیکر، یاد دہانی ایپس)۔

They allow more people to participate equally in school, work and society. Matlab یہ ہوا کہ There are four categories: Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: CategoryPurposeExamples 1. Mobility aidsHelp people move from one place to another.Smart wheelchairs, stair lifts 2. Sensory aidsSupport vision and hearing to improve interaction.Hearing aids, screen readers (VoiceOver), Braille displays 3. Communication aidsAssist individuals with speech difficulties to express themselves.Speech-generating devices, text-to-speech apps 4. Cognitive / learning aidsHelp people with memory, reading and understanding.Audiobooks, spell-checkers, digital reminder apps Mobility·Sensory·Communication·Cognitive A screen reader is software that reads aloud the text on a screen, so a blind person can use a phone or computer. VoiceOver is Apple's screen reader; Android has TalkBack. A Braille display is a device with small pins that rise and fall to form Braille dots, so a blind user can read screen text with their fingers. A speech-generating device speaks out words that a person types or selects on a screen. A smart wheelchair can be controlled by a joystick, voice or head movement and may avoid obstacles with sensors. Worked example sketchnote 1: Scenario — choose the right assistive technology: Worked example sketchnote 2: (a) Ahmed, a student in Hyderabad, is blind and wants to read his e-textbook. → Sensory aid: a screen reader or Braille display. Worked example sketchnote 3: (b) Mrs Rashida cannot climb the stairs of her house after a knee operation. → Mobility aid: stair lift (or smart wheelchair). Worked example sketchnote 4: (c) Zain cannot speak clearly due to a medical condition but can type. → Communication aid: text-to-speech app or speech-generating device. Worked example sketchnote 5: (d) Nani often forgets to take her medicine. → Cognitive aid: digital reminder app. Worked example sketchnote 6: (e) Usman has dyslexia (difficulty reading). → Cognitive/learning aid: audiobooks and spell-checkers. Worked example sketchnote 7: Method: identify the limitation (moving, seeing/hearing, speaking, memory/reading) → choose the matching category. Yaad rakhna: Four categories = "My Small Cat Cries": Mobility, Sensory, Communication, Cognitive. Link each to a body function: legs (mobility), eyes/ears (sensory), mouth (communication), mind (cognitive). Common mistake: Mistake: Putting text-to-speech and screen readers in the same category every time. Fix: In the source, the screen reader is a sensory aid (supports vision), while a text-to-speech app is listed as a communication aid (helps a person with speech difficulty express themselves). Decide by whose problem it solves. topics.title: 5.5.1 Importance of Assistive Technologies
topics.learn: Assistive technologies are important for three main reasons: Equal access to education: Screen readers allow blind students to read digital textbooks equally with their peers (classmates). Independence in daily life: Mobility aids reduce the need for constant human assistance — a person in a smart wheelchair can go to the market without someone pushing. Social inclusion: They break down barriers, allowing individuals to work, study and socialise confidently.

topics.title: 5.5.2 Career Connection in Assistive Tech
topics.learn: Designing assistive technology is a highly rewarding career path — you earn a living while improving people's lives. UX means user experience (how easy and pleasant a product is to use); UI means user interface (the screens and buttons you interact with). Accessibility means designing so that everyone, including people with disabilities, can use it.

topics.title: 6.1 Introduction to Digital Literacy
topics.learn: Digital literacy is the ability to understand and use digital devices, the internet, and online tools in a safe, effective, and responsible manner. Look at the three key words: In our increasingly digital world, digital literacy is essential for everyone, not only for computer experts. It enables you to: Safe – you protect yourself and others online (for example, you do not share passwords or private details). Effective – you get the job done well (for example, you find the right information quickly). Responsible – you use information honestly and fairly (for example, you do not copy someone else's work or spread false news). find information, communicate with others, produce digital content, and solve problems through technology.

topics.title: 6.2 Digital Literacy in the Information Age
topics.learn: The Information Age is the period we live in now, where vast amounts of data are produced, shared and accessed instantly through the internet, mobile devices and digital platforms (websites, apps, social media). Simply having access to technology is not enough. Owning a smartphone does not make you good at using information. You must develop the skills to understand, manage and use information wisely. Digital literacy goes beyond basic computer skills. It involves three kinds of ability: Together these abilities help you function successfully in a digital society.

topics.title: 6.3 Types of Data
topics.learn: Data means facts, numbers, words or observations that we collect. The data gathered through a survey, an investigation or a classroom project can be described in two ways: qualitatively or quantitatively. Knowing the difference is critical, because each type is analysed in a different way. Going a little further (background). Quantitative data is sometimes split into two kinds: Also note: a question with fixed categories (e.g. "Which activity do you use your phone for most? Lectures / Notes / Social media / Games") gives categories that you can count. In this chapter's case study such answers are treated as quantitative (categories), because you count how many students chose each option. Discrete data can only take separate, countable values, e.g. number of students in a class (35, 36 – never 35.5). Continuous data can take any value in a range and is measured, e.g. height (162.4 cm) or time online (2.75 hours).

Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: 6.3.1 Qualitative Data Qualitative data describes what people think, feel, notice or experience. It is non-numerical and descriptive: it is made of words, not numbers. The word comes from quality (what something is like). Examples: students' opinions about online classes; descriptions of study habits; observation notes ("The students looked bored after 20 minutes"). 6.3.2 Quantitative Data Quantitative data deals with numbers. The word comes from quantity (how much or how many). It is useful when you need to count, measure, compare, calculate averages, or display results in charts. Examples: number of students using the internet daily; marks obtained in a test; time spent online in hours. 6.3.3 Comparing Qualitative and Quantitative Data Type of dataNatureExamplesBest used for QualitativeDescriptive, non-numericalOpinions, reasons, behaviourUnderstanding why and how something happens QuantitativeNumerical, countable or measurableHours, scores, percentages, totalsComparing results and making graphs/charts Worked example sketchnote 1: Classify each piece of data. Worked example sketchnote 2: Quick test: ask "Can I calculate an average of this?" If yes, it is quantitative. If the answer is words, it is qualitative. Yaad rakhna: QUALitative = QUALity = words and feelings. QUANTitative = QUANTity = numbers and counts. Qualitative answers why/how; quantitative answers how many/how much. Common mistake: Mistake: Thinking that any data containing a number is quantitative. A phone number or a roll number is a label, not a quantity – averaging roll numbers is meaningless. Fix: Data is quantitative only if the number measures or counts something. topics.title: 6.4.1 – 6.4.2 Interviews and Surveys
topics.learn: An interview is a planned conversation used to gather information directly from a person. Strength: you get deep, detailed answers and can ask follow-up questions ("Why do you say that?"). Weakness: it takes a lot of time, so you can only interview a few people. It may be one-to-one (you and one person) or in a small group. Questions are planned in advance, so you do not forget anything important. Answers are usually qualitative (opinions, reasons, experiences). A survey (or questionnaire) is useful when the same set of questions needs to be asked to many people. It may be on paper or created with digital tools such as Google Forms or Microsoft Forms. Note: online survey tools automatically collect responses and display basic charts, which makes data analysis much easier.

topics.title: 6.4.3 – 6.4.5 Prototypes, Observation and Simulations
topics.learn: A prototype is a simple early version of a product, model or solution. It allows an idea to be tested before time and effort are spent on the final version. Users try the prototype and give feedback, and this feedback becomes useful data for improvement. Example: Before building a full school app, you draw the screens on paper (or make a few clickable screens in a design tool) and ask five classmates to try "finding the timetable". You note where they get confused. In observation, the researcher watches what people do or what happens in a situation and records the results carefully. No direct questions are asked. The data may be qualitative (written notes, e.g. "students push in the queue") or quantitative (counts, e.g. "42 students bought samosas in 10 minutes"). Why use it? People sometimes say one thing and do another. Observation shows what really happens. A simulation is a computer-based model of a real situation. Variables (the things that can change, like speed, temperature or number of people) can be changed to see what happens. Simulations are highly useful when real experiments are costly, risky or difficult to perform. Examples: a flight simulator for training pilots (real crashes are dangerous); a traffic simulation to test what happens if a new signal is added (changing real roads is costly); a weather model to predict a cyclone (you cannot experiment with real weather).

topics.title: 6.5 Primary and Secondary Data
topics.learn: Whenever you use data, it is important to know where it came from. The source affects how much control the researcher had over collecting it, and how confidently the results can be used.
topics.urdu: بنیادی ڈیٹا (Primary Data) محقق خود کسی خاص مقصد کے لیے براہِ راست جمع کرتا ہے، مثلاً سروے، انٹرویو یا مشاہدہ۔ ثانوی ڈیٹا (Secondary Data) پہلے ہی کسی اور نے جمع کیا ہوتا ہے اور اسے نئے مقصد کے لیے دوبارہ استعمال کیا جاتا ہے، جیسے کتابیں، رپورٹس اور آن لائن ڈیٹا بیس۔ بنیادی ڈیٹا پر محقق کا کنٹرول زیادہ اور ثانوی ڈیٹا پر کم ہوتا ہے۔

It is gathered directly from people, events or situations, rather than taken from an already published source. Sources: interviews, surveys, observations, experiments. 6.5.2 Secondary Data Secondary data has already been collected by someone else and is being used again for a new purpose. It is taken from existing archives (stored collections of information). Sources: books, research articles, official reports, web statistics, online databases. ControlHigh control over questions and collection process.Limited control because the data a Worked example sketchnote 1: Primary or secondary? Hira is researching "Internet use among students in Hyderabad". topics.title: 6.6 Designing a Data-Collection Approach
topics.learn: Before collecting data, a researcher must have a plan. A plan makes sure that the information gathered is accurate, relevant (related to the question) and useful. Follow these eight steps in order: Define the research question clearly. What exactly do you want to find out? Decide the type of data needed: quantitative, qualitative, or both. Select suitable methods (survey, interview, observation). Choose the sample or target group – the people who will give you data. Prepare the tools such as forms, questions and observation sheets. Collect the data carefully and accurately. Store the data digitally in a spreadsheet and keep a backup. Follow ethical practice and respect privacy. Consent is mandatory (you must get permission).

Board کے لیے یہ line important ہے: Collect the data carefully and accurately. دیکھو، sketchnote پہ لکھا ہے: Store the data digitally in a spreadsheet and keep a backup. Matlab یہ ہوا کہ Follow ethical practice and respect privacy. Consent is mandatory (you must get permission). Data type: Both – quantitative (number of taps left running, minutes) and qualitative (reasons students give). Worked example sketchnote 4: 3. Methods: Observation (count running taps) + a short survey (ask about habits). Worked example sketchnote 5: 4. Sample: All 12 taps in the college; 30 students from different classes for the survey.
