topics.title: 6.7 Presenting Data Using Digital Tools: 6.7.1 Spreadsheets and 6.7.2 Presentations
topics.learn: Collecting data is only one part of the work. You must also present your findings so that others can understand them quickly and easily. Digital tools make this much easier. The four main tools are spreadsheets, presentations, infographics and reports. Spreadsheets such as MS Excel, Google Sheets and Apple Numbers arrange information in rows (horizontal, numbered 1, 2, 3…) and columns (vertical, lettered A, B, C…). The box where a row and column meet is a cell, named by its column and row, e.g. B2. With a spreadsheet you can: A formula always starts with =. A range such as B2:B4 means "cells B2 to B4". Enter data systematically (one record per row). Calculate totals, averages and percentages. Sort (arrange in order) and filter (show only some rows) records. Create charts and graphs automatically. Presentation software such as PowerPoint, Google Slides and Canva helps you explain findings to an audience in an organised way. Good practice: Spreadsheets and presentations work together: you make a chart from the spreadsheet data and insert it into the slides. Begin with a clear title and the research question. Use short bullet points instead of long paragraphs. Include tables, charts and key findings. Keep the design simple and readable (large font, few colours).

topics.title: 6.7.3 – 6.7.4 Infographics and Reports
topics.learn: An infographic (information + graphic) is a visual way of presenting information, facts or data so that people can understand the main idea quickly and easily. Tools such as Canva, Power BI or Tableau can be used. A good infographic should: Simplify complex concepts. Highlight the most important findings and results. Use clear visuals, limited text and accurate information. Reports are structured documents used to present collected data, findings, analysis and conclusions. Tools like MS Word or Google Docs are standard. A good report should: Optional: you may use AI tools carefully to improve wording, but always review for accuracy. AI can make mistakes or invent facts, and you are responsible for what you submit. Start with a clear title, introduction and purpose. Present the collected data using tables or charts. Explain findings in simple language. Include conclusions and recommendations based on the data. Visual rule of thumb: a good chart or infographic can explain complex data faster than a long paragraph. However, visuals must always be accurate and based strictly on the real data collected – never exaggerated.

topics.title: 6.8 Case Study: Digital Inquiry Project
topics.learn: This case study shows how to apply all the ideas of this chapter to solve a real-world problem from start to finish. An inquiry is an investigation to find the answer to a question. Research question: "How does daily mobile phone use affect the study habits of students?" Scenario: Students notice classmates using phones during free periods and while studying. Some say phones help them learn; others say phones waste time. The class must investigate whether phone use helps or harms study habits.

topics.title: 6.8 Steps 1 – 3: Advanced Search and Methodology
topics.learn: Students first search for background information using search engines (such as Google or Bing). They use advanced search operators – special symbols or words typed into the search box – to narrow down results and find reliable secondary data. Other useful operators (background): - (minus) excludes a word, e.g. phone addiction -game; OR finds either word, e.g. smartphone OR mobile; site:.gov.pk searches only Pakistani government websites. Source evaluation checklist. Before trusting a source, ask: Is the author/organisation clearly mentioned? Is the information recent? Is the website reliable (.edu, .gov, research-based)? Does the source provide facts/references, or is it biased (one-sided, trying to sell something)? Students decide what kind of primary data they will collect: Quantitative: number of hours used daily; percentage who feel distracted. Qualitative: opinions on why they get distracted; suggestions for better use. Because they need to ask the same questions to many students, a survey/questionnaire (via Google Forms or on paper) is the most efficient method. Interviews would take too long for so many people, and observation could not reveal opinions.

Step 1: Perform advanced searches Step 2: Identify data types Step 3: Select data-collection methods Worked example sketchnote 1: Building a search query step by step. You want official PDF reports about screen time of students on Pakistani government websites. Worked example sketchnote 2: Step 1 – Plain search: screen time students → millions of results, many blogs and adverts. Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 2 – Exact phrase: "screen time" students → results must contain the exact phrase. Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3 – Only PDFs: "screen time" students filetype:pdf → mostly reports and papers. Worked example sketchnote 5: Step 4 – Only government sites: "screen time" students filetype:pdf site:.gov.pk → a small number of highly relevant, reliable results. Worked example sketchnote 6: Step 5 – Evaluate: open a result and check the checklist: author named? year recent? references given? Yaad rakhna: Three operators, three jobs: " " = exact, filetype: = format, site: = where. Note: there is no space after the colon (site:.edu, not site: .edu). Common mistake: Mistake: Assuming the first search result is the most reliable. Search results can be adverts or popular blogs. Fix: Always apply the source evaluation checklist. A website ending in .edu or .gov is usually more reliable, but you should still check the date and author. topics.title: 6.8 Steps 4 – 6: Survey Preparation and Primary Data Collection
topics.learn: Design clear, unbiased questions. Each question is linked to the type of data it produces: The sample is the group of people who provide the data. It is usually impossible to ask everyone (the whole population), so a smaller group is chosen. The students decide to survey 40 Class XI students from different sections to get a representative mix of habits. "Representative" means the sample looks like the whole group – it includes different kinds of students, not just your friends. Ethics means doing what is morally right. When conducting the survey, students must follow strict ethical guidelines: Ask permission before collecting responses (consent). Avoid collecting sensitive personal information. Do not record names unless absolutely necessary (anonymity). Keep the responses private. Use the data only for educational purposes.

topics.title: 6.8 Steps 7 – 9: Secondary Data and Spreadsheet Organisation
topics.learn: Students include a reliable online article stating that "excessive screen time lowers concentration." They will compare this secondary data with their own primary survey results. If both agree, the conclusion is stronger. If they disagree, the students must think about why (for example, a different age group or country). Responses are entered into MS Excel or Google Sheets to sort, calculate totals and find averages. Each row is one student; each column is one question. (The full sheet has 40 rows, one per student. The formulas for this table are worked out in topic 6.7.1.) The spreadsheet data is converted into visuals to make it easy to digest. In the source, the "Daily Phone Use (Hours)" bar chart groups the 40 students into three bars: 1–3 hrs, 3–5 hrs and 5+ hrs, with the 3–5 hrs bar the tallest.

Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: Step 7: Use secondary data Step 8: Organise data in a spreadsheet Step 9: Create charts and graphs Daily Phone Use (Hours) 0 8 16 24 12 21 7 1–3 hrs 3–5 hrs 5+ hrs Students Bar chart of daily phone use for 40 students. The counts (12, 21, 7) are estimated from the bar heights in the source chart. Worked example sketchnote 1: Making the chart in Google Sheets. Worked example sketchnote 2: Step 1 – Count each group. If the hours are in B2:B41, use =COUNTIF(B2:B41,"<3") for under 3 hrs, =COUNTIFS(B2:B41,">=3",B2:B41,"<5") for 3 to under 5 hrs, and =COUNTIF(B2:B41,">=5") for 5 hrs or more. (This gives non-overlapping groups.) Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 2 – Check the total. 12 + 21 + 7 = 40 ✓ – every student is counted exactly once. Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3 – Percentages. 12 ÷ 40 = 30%; 21 ÷ 40 = 52.5%; 7 ÷ 40 = 17.5%. Total = 100% ✓. Worked example sketchnote 5: Step 4 – Insert chart. Select the group labels and counts → Insert → Chart → choose Column chart. Add the title "Daily Phone Use (Hours)" and label the axes. Worked example sketchnote 6: Step 5 – Choose the right chart. topics.title: 6.8 Steps 10 – 12: Data Analysis, Conclusion and Recommendations
topics.learn: To analyse means to study the data carefully to find patterns and trends. By looking at the spreadsheet and charts, the group identifies: Most students (the majority) use phones for 3–5 hours daily. Half use it for educational purposes (lectures/notes). A clear trend: students who use phones mostly for entertainment report much higher distraction levels than those who use them for study. A conclusion answers the research question using the evidence: "The research shows mobile phones have both positive and negative effects. They provide access to learning materials. However, excessive use of social media and gaming reduces concentration. Therefore, phones should not be banned, but managed wisely." Recommendations are practical suggestions based on the data. The students recommend: Turn off social media notifications while studying. Set daily screen-time limits. Take physical breaks from screens to protect health.
topics.urdu: دسویں قدم میں چارٹس اور اسپریڈشیٹ سے رجحانات تلاش کیے جاتے ہیں: زیادہ تر طلبہ روزانہ تین سے پانچ گھنٹے فون استعمال کرتے ہیں، نصف اسے تعلیم کے لیے استعمال کرتے ہیں، اور تفریح کے لیے استعمال کرنے والے زیادہ توجہ بٹنے کی شکایت کرتے ہیں۔ گیارہویں قدم میں نتیجہ لکھا جاتا ہے کہ فون پر پابندی نہیں بلکہ اس کا دانشمندانہ استعمال ہونا چاہیے۔ بارہویں قدم میں سفارشات دی جاتی ہیں: پڑھائی کے دوران نوٹیفکیشن بند کریں، اسکرین ٹائم کی حد مقرر کریں اور وقفے لیں۔

Using the estimated chart counts (12, 21, 7 out of 40): Worked example sketchnote 2: Step 1: 21 ÷ 40 = 52.5%. Since 52.5% > 50%, the statement "most students use phones for 3–5 hours" is supported. Formula: =COUNTIF(D2:D41,"Lectures")+COUNTIF(D2:D41,"Notes"). Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 3 – Compare groups: filter the sheet to show only Social Media/Games users and count how many said "Yes" to distracted; then do the same for Lectures/Notes users. Worked example sketchnote 5: Step 4 – Link to secondary data: the article said excessive screen time lowers concentration; the survey agrees, so the conclusion is stronger. topics.title: 6.8 The Final Digital Artefact
topics.learn: A digital artefact is a final product created using digital technologies. Students must create one final artefact that answers the original research question. It is not just a decorated file; it must present evidence and conclusions. A dashboard is an interactive screen of charts; the viewer can click filters (e.g. "show only Commerce students") and the charts update.

Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: Standard artefact structure Title Research Question Introduction Method of Data Collection Primary Data Findings Secondary Data Summary Charts and Graphs Conclusion Recommendations References Worked example sketchnote 1: Planning a 10-slide presentation artefact for the phone study (one slide per structure item): Worked example sketchnote 2: Slide 1 Title: "Phones and Study Habits – Class XI Survey". Slide 2 Research question. Slide 3 Introduction: why the class investigated this. Slide 4 Method: Google Form survey, 40 students, different sections, anonymous with consent. Slide 5 Primary findings: 52.5% use phones 3–5 hours; half use for study. Slide 6 Secondary data: article on screen time and concentration. Slide 7 The bar chart of daily phone use. Slide 8 Conclusion: "manage wisely, don't ban". Slide 9 Three recommendations. Slide 10 References: the article's title, author, website and date. Yaad rakhna: The structure follows the inquiry itself: What (title, question, intro) → How (method) → Found (primary, secondary, charts) → So what (conclusion, recommendations) → Credit (references). Common mistake: Mistake: Spending all your time on colours and animations and forgetting evidence. Fix: An artefact is judged on whether it answers the research question with evidence. Also never skip References – listing your secondary sources is honest and avoids plagiarism. Exam میں یہ terms English میں ہی لکھو: digital artefact, one final artefact, not just a decorated file, evidence, conclusions, dashboard, Slide 1, Slide 2, Slide 3, Slide 4, Slide 5, Slide 6۔ ان کا مکمل Urdu ترجمہ examiner نہیں مانگتا۔ Board پہ سوال یوں آتا ہے: Learn the four artefact options with tools and purpose (a table question), and the ten-part structure in order. "What is a digital artefact?" – stress that it must present evidence and conclusions, not just decoration. Answer میں Definition، Explain، Example، Diagram اور Working لکھنا۔ اللہ حافظ۔

topics.title: 1.1 Fundamentals of Human-Computer Interaction
topics.learn: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is the study and design of technology so that it serves people. An HCI system is easy to use, efficient, and responsive to human needs. HCI is also known as CHI (Computer-Human Interface) or MMI (Man-Machine Interaction). The three names mean the same idea: the meeting point of a person and a machine. HCI is not only "making a pretty screen". It asks: Can a student in Hyderabad find results on the school portal in 30 seconds? Can a grandmother send JazzCash without help? Can a person standing at an outdoor ATM in bright sunlight read the buttons?
topics.urdu: ہیومن کمپیوٹر انٹریکشن (HCI) کا مطلب ہے ٹیکنالوجی کو اس طرح ڈیزائن کرنا کہ وہ انسانوں کے لیے فائدہ مند، آسان اور مؤثر ہو۔ اسے CHI یا MMI بھی کہتے ہیں۔ انسان اور کمپیوٹر پانچ حسّی راستوں سے بات کرتے ہیں: بصارت، چھونا، سننا، آواز اور مکانی حرکت۔ ہیپٹکس (Haptics) وہ ارتعاش ہے جو آپ کو چھو کر محسوس ہوتا ہے۔
topics.spokenUrdu: Students, السلام علیکم۔ آج کا lecture sketchnote Urdish میں ہے — poori topic ki in-depth explanation. An HCI system is easy to use, efficient, and responsive to human needs. HCI is also known as CHI (Computer-Human Interface) or MMI (Man-Machine Interaction). The three names mean the same idea: the meeting point of a person and a machine. Matlab یہ ہوا کہ HCI is not only "making a pretty screen". It asks: Can a student in Hyderabad find results on the school portal in 30 seconds? Can a grandmother send JazzCash without help? Can a person standing at an outdoor ATM in bright sunlight read the buttons? Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: Sensory channels of interaction Humans and computers communicate through sensory channels. A sensory channel is a path that carries information to (or from) one of the human senses. Computers must send and receive signals on the same channels, or the conversation breaks. ChannelHow humans use itHow computers respond Sight (بصارت)Look at screens, graphics or videos.Displays visuals on monitors and screens. Touch (چھونا)Tap, type or swipe.Responds with clicks or vibrations (haptics). Hearing (سننا)Listen to sounds or voices.Provides audio feedback via speakers. Voice (آواز)Speak commands (for example, "Alexa").Processes speech and replies. Spatial (مکانی)Move in physical space.Tracks position or body movement (for example, VR). Haptics means physical feedback you can feel, such as a phone vibrating when a JazzCash payment succeeds. Spatial interaction means the system notices where your body is, as in a VR headset or a Kinect camera. Sight Touch HUMAN senses Hearing Voice Spatial Five sensory channels meet at the human. HCI design must support the channels the user actually needs. Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: map a JazzCash payment to channels. Sara in Sukkur sends Rs 500 to her brother. Worked example sketchnote 2: If the app showed no tick, no sound and no vibration, Sara would not know whether the money left. That is an HCI failure, not a banking failure. Worked example sketchnote 3: Sight: she looks at the JazzCash home screen and the amount field. Worked example sketchnote 4: Touch: she taps "Send Money" and types the mobile number. Worked example sketchnote 5: Voice (optional): she could say "JazzCash, send five hundred rupees" if voice commands are on. Worked example sketchnote 6: Hearing + haptics: a beep and a short vibration confirm "Payment successful". Yaad rakhna: Remember the three names: HCI = CHI = MMI. Think "Human meets Machine." Five channels: S-T-H-V-S — Sight, Touch, Hearing, Voice, Spatial. "See The Handy Voice in Space." Common mistake: Mistake: Writing "HCI is only about computer hardware" or mixing up Voice with Hearing. Fix: HCI is about the design of the conversation between people and machines. Hearing is what you listen to (speakers). Voice is what you speak (microphone + speech software). topics.title: 1.1.1 Traditional Interaction and 1.1.2 Natural Interaction
topics.learn: 1.1.1 Traditional interaction is the basic way people use everyday devices. It relies on standard input and output: a mouse, a keyboard, a keypad, a monitor, speakers, or a simple touchscreen tap and swipe. 1.1.2 Natural interaction is advanced, smart technology that lets people interact without a mouse or keyboard. It feels more human — you speak, move, or show your face, and the system understands. Computer: moving a mouse and typing on a keyboard; output via monitor and speakers. Smartphone (traditional use): tapping and swiping on a touchscreen; output via screen lighting and vibrations. Voice: speaking commands into a device (for example, "Alexa, play a song"). Body and gesture: facial recognition to unlock a phone, or playing VR games by waving hands.

topics.title: 1.2 Applications of HCI (Domains of Life)
topics.learn: HCI is used to design and develop interactive systems such as desktop applications, websites and mobile apps. These are human-centred solutions built to meet user needs across many domains of life. A domain is an area of daily activity — health, money, school, talking to people. When you design for a domain, you design for that domain's users, tasks and risks. A mistake on a games app is annoying. A mistake on a medical or banking screen can harm a person or lose money. That is why examiners treat this topic as golden.

topics.title: 1.3 Components of HCI
topics.learn: HCI relies on several primary components that work together. If one component is weak, the whole interaction feels broken. The first four are the people, the machine, the conversation, and the job to be done.
topics.urdu: ایچ سی آئی کے چار بنیادی اجزاء ہیں: صارف (اینڈ یوزر جو خود سسٹم چلاتا ہے اور اسٹیک ہولڈر جس کا نتیجے میں مفاد ہے)، کمپیوٹر سسٹم (ان پٹ، آؤٹ پٹ اور فیڈبیک کا پلیٹ فارم)، صارف کا تعامل (کلک، ٹیپ، ٹائپ، بولنا) اور کام (ٹاسک) جس کی پیچیدگی، مطلوبہ مہارت اور وقت مختلف ہوتا ہے۔ اے ٹی ایم سے رقم نکالنا آسان اور مختصر کام ہے؛ پاسپورٹ کی آن لائن درخواست لمبا کام ہے۔

If one component is weak, the whole interaction feels broken. The first four are the people, the machine, the conversation, and the job to be done. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: ComponentMeaning iUser (صارف)Any individual or group that interacts with a computer system to achieve defined goals. Two categories: end users (people who directly operate the system, from beginners to experts) and stakeholders (people with an interest in the outcome, such as managers and clients). iiComputer system (کمپیوٹر سسٹم)The platform where humans and computers communicate through input, output and feedback using an interface. It connects human actions with machine responses. iiiUser interaction (صارف کا تعامل)The process through which a user communicates with a system by performing actions (clicking, tapping, typing, speaking). It transforms user intent into system responses. ivTask (کام)The specific action users perform (for example, booking a ticket). It has three characteristics: task complexity (filling a form vs designing a 3D model), user knowledge (basic typing vs advanced programming), and time requirement (ATM withdrawal vs online passport application). i) User End user / stakeholder iii) Interaction click, tap, type, speak ii) Computer input · output · feedback iv) Task complexity · skill · time HCI components work as one loop The user performs a task through int Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: label the four components of an HBL ATM withdrawal. Worked example sketchnote 2: User: end user = the account holder standing at the machine; stakeholder = the bank that owns the ATM and must keep it safe and working. Worked example sketchnote 3: Computer system: the ATM hardware plus the bank's software; it takes PIN input, shows a screen, and dispenses notes (output and feedback). Worked example sketchnote 4: User interaction: insert card → type PIN → choose "Cash" → type amount → confirm. Intent ("I want Rs 5,000") becomes a machine response (cash + receipt). Worked example sketchnote 5: Task: withdraw cash. Complexity: low (a few buttons). User knowledge: basic (PIN and amounts). Time: about one minute — much shorter than an online passport application. Yaad rakhna: U-C-I-T: User, Computer system, Interaction, Task. "U Can Interact with Tasks." Then add three task questions: How hard? What skill? How long? Common mistake: Mistake: Calling the bank manager an "end user" of the ATM, or saying a task has only one property (difficulty). Fix: The manager is usually a stakeholder. The person pressing the keys is the end user. A task always has complexity, knowledge and time — mention all three in long answers. topics.title: Types of User Interaction
topics.learn: User interaction can happen in many different ways depending on the technology used. Learn every type with one clean example — board questions often ask you to "list and explain" five or more.

Worked example sketchnote 2: Same idea on a school portal: menu-driven ("Date Sheet", "Fee Challan"), form fill (leave application), conversational (a chatbot "When is the chemistry practical?"). Worked example sketchnote 3: Open the app with a fingerprint → biometric. Worked example sketchnote 4: Home screen shows Send Money, Bill Payment, Load → you tap Send Money → menu-driven. Worked example sketchnote 5: Type the receiver's mobile number and the amount → form fill. Worked example sketchnote 6: The keypad vibrates on each tap → haptic. Worked example sketchnote 7: Optional: say "Send five hundred to Ali" then tap Confirm → multimodal (voice + touch). Yaad rakhna: Group them: hands on screen (direct, gesture, haptic) · words (command, conversational, voice) · lists and blanks (menu, form) · automatic/body (context-aware, biometric) · mix (multimodal). topics.title: Interface Types, Environment and Feedback
topics.learn: Components v–vii complete the HCI picture: the look of the controls, the place where you use them, and the signals that tell you "it worked" or "try again". The user interface is the medium through which humans interact with computer systems. The environment is the real-world setting where a person uses a computer system. It is shaped by: Feedback is the signal or response given to confirm or guide actions. Graphical User Interface (GUI): visual elements such as windows, icons and menus (Windows OS, Android). Command-Line Interface (CLI): text-based typing (MS-DOS, Linux terminal). Touch interface: tapping, swiping, pinching (smartphones, tablets). Voice User Interface (VUI): spoken commands (smart speakers). Natural User Interface (NUI): gestures, body movements or immersive environments (VR headsets, Microsoft Kinect). Physical conditions — an ATM outdoors in sunlight, heat, noise, rain. Social conditions — a quiet classroom, a crowded bazaar, privacy at a PIN pad. Technical hardware — slow college Wi-Fi, a cracked phone screen, an old browser.
topics.urdu: یوزر انٹرفیس وہ واسطہ ہے جس سے انسان سسٹم سے بات کرتا ہے: GUI تصاویر اور مینو، CLI لکھی کمانڈ، ٹچ، آواز (VUI) اور قدرتی اشارے (NUI)۔ ماحول وہ حقیقی جگہ ہے جہاں سسٹم استعمال ہوتا ہے — دھوپ میں اے ٹی ایم، خاموش کلاس روم، کمزور وائی فائی۔ سسٹم فیڈبیک مشین کا جواب ہے ("بھیج دیا گیا")؛ صارف کا فیڈبیک صارف کا ان پٹ ہے (سبمٹ بٹن یا پانچ ستارے)۔

Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: System feedback Response from the computer: a "Loading…" bar, a "Message Sent!" tick, or an error sound. Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: environment and feedback at a roadside ATM in Hyderabad. Worked example sketchnote 2: Physical: noon sunlight washes out a dim screen — the GUI must use high contrast. Worked example sketchnote 3: Social: people stand in a queue; the user needs a privacy shield around the PIN pad. Worked example sketchnote 4: Technical: the printer may be out of paper, so on-screen "Take your cash" plus a beep still has to confirm the transaction. Worked example sketchnote 5: System feedback: "Please wait", cash coming out, a printed or SMS receipt. Worked example sketchnote 6: User feedback: the user presses Confirm, or later rates the bank's app 4 stars. Worked example sketchnote 7: On a school portal during board-exam week, hundreds of students on weak Wi-Fi need a visible "Loading results…" bar. Silence after clicking "View marks" is poor system feedback. Yaad rakhna: GUI vs CLI vs NUI: GUI = pictures you click. CLI = words you type. NUI = body you move. VUI = voice you speak. Touch = fingers on glass. Feedback rule: system talks back; user talks in. Common mistake: Mistake: Mixing up system feedback with user feedback, or saying "environment" means only the software theme (dark mode). Fix: A tick mark is system feedback. A 5-star rating is user feedback. Environment is the real world around the user — sun, noise, hardware — not the colour of the app (though a good UI will adapt to that world). topics.title: 1.4 Importance of HCI
topics.learn: HCI ensures that machines are approachable and usable, turning complex technology into everyday tools. Good design makes technology simple and enjoyable (touchscreens). Poor design causes confusion and risks (unclear buttons on medical devices). This is why HCI is not optional decoration. A confusing JazzCash confirm button can send money to the wrong number. A confusing school-portal "Submit" can lock a student out of an online exam. Importance questions in the board exam expect the five implications below, each with a sentence of explanation.
topics.urdu: اچھا ایچ سی آئی پیچیدہ ٹیکنالوجی کو روزمرہ کا آسان اوزار بناتا ہے؛ برا ڈیزائن الجھن اور خطرہ پیدا کرتا ہے، جیسے طبی آلے پر غیر واضح بٹن۔ پانچ مضمرات: پیداوری بڑھتی ہے، شمولیت آتی ہے، جدت اپنائی جاتی ہے، معیشت مضبوط ہوتی ہے، اور رازداری و انصاف کی اخلاقی ذمہ داری پوری ہوتی ہے۔

topics.title: 1.5 Accessibility Principles
topics.learn: Accessibility principles are HCI guidelines that ensure digital systems are usable by all individuals, including people with diverse physical, sensory and cognitive abilities. They remove barriers to create equal access. Accessibility is not a "special extra". It is how you make sure a student with low vision, a shopkeeper who cannot use a mouse, or a colour-blind driver can still complete the task.

topics.title: 1.6 Need Analysis for Interface Design
topics.learn: Need analysis is the process of identifying the gap between the existing situation and the desired outcome. In HCI it is done before designing a UI, so that you understand users' goals, tasks, abilities and expectations. If you skip need analysis, you guess. Guessing is how a school portal ends up with 40 menus and no "Download date sheet" button on the home screen.

topics.title: 1.7 Human-Computer Interaction Problems
topics.learn: HCI problems are common difficulties that stop users from using technology smoothly. They happen when systems fail to meet human needs or cognitive limits. Cognitive limits means the mind can only hold and process so much at once — if an app asks you to remember three SMS codes at the same time, it has gone past that limit. Board answers score well when you name the problem, explain it in one line, and give a concrete example (the source examples are safe; a matching local example is even better).

topics.title: 1.8 Methods for Improving HCI
topics.learn: Once you can name an HCI problem, you fix it with a matching method. The source lists eight methods. Learn each with its tiny example — they pair almost one-to-one with Section 1.7. User-centred design (UCD) means the real user's goals drive every decision, and you trial (pilot-test) the design with those users instead of guessing in an office. Responsive design means the layout rearranges itself for phone, tablet and PC, instead of staying a laptop-only page. Enhance usability: simplify navigation (a clear "Buy Now" button). Strengthen accessibility: support disabilities (captions on videos). Ensure consistency: keep layouts uniform (the same "Save" button everywhere). Provide clear feedback: show action results ("Payment Successful" popup). Improve adaptability: responsive design (the website scales to mobile screens). Apply user-centred design (UCD): focus on real user goals and pilot-test. Use multimodal interaction: allow touch, voice or gesture inputs combined. Continuous testing: regularly update based on user feedback.

topics.title: 1.9 User Interface Design (UI vs UX)
topics.learn: UI design is the process of creating and organizing the visual elements of a software application so users can interact with it easily and efficiently. UX is the overall experience a user has while interacting with a system — how smooth, comfortable and satisfying it feels. UI is what you see; UX is how it feels.

topics.title: 1.9.3–1.9.5 Wireframing, Figma and Prototypes
topics.learn: 1.9.3 Wireframing is creating a basic visual outline or blueprint of a user interface before the final design. It plans the structure without focusing on colours or detailed graphics. Low-fidelity wireframes (Lo-Fi) A simple black-and-white sketch showing basic layout (boxes and lines). Used early to test and share ideas quickly. Focuses purely on structure and flow. High-fidelity prototypes (Hi-Fi) A detailed version that looks almost exactly like the final product. Includes real colours, fonts, images and interactive clickable buttons. Used for final user testing.

topics.title: 1.11 Test and Evaluate HCI (Evaluation Methods)
topics.learn: Testing checks if the product works properly (finding bugs). Evaluation determines whether it meets users' needs (usability). Together they improve the product before release. A school portal can be "bug-free" (testing passed) and still unusable if students cannot find the date sheet (evaluation failed). You need both.

NPS (Net Promoter Score)Asks users: "How likely are you to recommend this app to a friend?" Measures user loyalty. Formative evaluationDone during development to collect early feedback and improve the design continuously. Summative evaluationDone at the end of development to measure overall success against the original goals. Expert reviewsUsability specialists review the app against established design standards (heuristics). Heuristics are agreed rules of good design (for example "show system status", "be consistent"). Worked example sketchnote 3: A teacher who has studied HCI checks the screens against standard rules (Is feedback visible? Are labels consistent?). That is an expert review. topics.title: 1.11.2 Testing Methods (Usability, A/B, Automated)
topics.learn: Testing involves observing how the system behaves under specific conditions. Learn all seven methods. The three named in the heading — usability, A/B and automated — are the ones examiners ask most, but a complete answer also names the others. Usability testing: observing real users while they perform realistic tasks, to measure efficiency and satisfaction. If the user gets stuck, designers know where to fix the UI. Task-based testing: assigning a specific task (for example, "Find a product and add it to cart") and strictly measuring completion time, success rate and number of errors. Automated audits: software bots scan websites to detect technical issues such as broken links, slow loading speeds or low colour contrast. A/B testing: comparing two versions of an interface (A and B). Half the users see A, half see B. The one with more clicks or sign-ups wins. Compatibility testing: verifying the system on different browsers (Chrome, Safari), devices (mobiles, tablets, PCs) and operating systems. Performance and load testing: simulating high traffic (for example 10,000 users logging in at once) to see if speed drops or the server crashes. Keyboard and screen-reader walkthroughs: navigating using only the keyboard (Tab/Enter) or assistive technologies, to check accessibility for users with disabilities.

Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: test JazzCash "Send Money" and a school portal with numbers. Worked example sketchnote 2: Usability testing. Sit beside five students. Task: "Send Rs 100 to this test number." Do not help. Note where they pause. If three people look for Confirm at the bottom and it is at the top, that is your UI fix. Worked example sketchnote 3: Task-based testing (numbers). Same task for 10 students. Worked example sketchnote 4: A/B testing. Version A: green "Send" at the top. Version B: large orange "Send" under the amount. 200 users each. If B gets 140 completed payments and A gets 90, B wins. You keep B. Worked example sketchnote 5: Automated audit. A bot reports 3 broken "Fee challan" links and low contrast on the portal's grey-on-grey marks table. Fix those before the board-exam rush. Worked example sketchnote 6: Load testing. On result day, 10,000 students log in at 9:00 a.m. If the server crashes, performance testing failed — the UI never even appears. Worked example sketchnote 7: Keyboard walkthrough. Unplug the mouse. High errors + high time = poor HCI, even if most people eventually succeed. Yaad rakhna: Task-based three numbers: Time, Success, Errors. A/B: two versions, split users, the higher clicks/sign-ups win. Bot: links, speed, contrast. Load: many users at once. Keyboard: Tab and Enter only. topics.title: 2.1 Analyze algorithms for correctness
topics.learn: An algorithm is correct if its output matches the expected results for a given input. Analysing correctness means showing that the algorithm produces the intended output for all valid inputs, not just one lucky example. Two methods are used in this course:

topics.title: 2.1.1 Trace Tables
topics.learn: A trace table is a technique used to monitor how the values of variables change during the execution of an algorithm. It is a paper execution of the code — a manual walkthrough, also called a dry run. You act as the computer and fill in one row after another. Purpose of trace tables Components of a trace table Dry running: execute the algorithm line by line by hand. Debugging: find logical errors where the algorithm runs but the output is wrong. Validation: check that the algorithm does what it is intended to do. Line / step number — which line is being executed. Variables — one column for every variable. Input / output — user inputs and printed results. Condition check — True/False for IF, WHILE, FOR, and similar tests.

Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: soldiers who meet the height rule. To qualify for training, a soldier’s height must be between 1.57 and 1.91 metres, inclusive. Worked example sketchnote 2: Inputs: all soldiers’ heights. Output: the count of eligible soldiers. Worked example sketchnote 3: Step 1: Start Step 2: SET Total = 0 Step 3: Set AllHeights = [1.91, 2.01, 1.87, 1.57, 1.48] Step 4: FOR EACH height FROM AllHeights DO Step 5: IF height >= 1.57 AND height <= 1.91 THEN Step 6: SET Total = Total + 1 Step 7: END IF Step 8: END FOR EACH Step 9: Print Total Step 10: End Worked example sketchnote 4: Inclusive means the two boundary values count: 1.57 and 1.91 are eligible. Worked example sketchnote 5: Eligible: 1.91, 1.87, 1.57. Not eligible: 2.01 (above 1.91) and 1.48 (below 1.57). Printed Total = 3. Yaad rakhna: How to fill a trace table without getting lost. Write a new row every time a variable changes or a condition is tested. Copy unchanged values into the new row so you never guess. Circle the final output. Mnemonic: V-I-C-O — Variables, Input, Condition, Output. If a column is missing, the table is incomplete. Common mistake: Mistake 1: treating 1.57 or 1.91 as out of range. The words “inclusive” and the operators >= and <= mean the boundaries are allowed. Mistake 2: updating Total on a False condition. If the IF is False, skip the SET line and leave Total unchanged. Mistake 3: writing only the last Total. Examiners award marks for the changing values in the table, not only for the printed 3. topics.title: 2.1.2 Stepwise Reasoning
topics.learn: Stepwise reasoning (also called logic verification) breaks an algorithm into logical sections and checks the state of the algorithm at each stage. A state is a snapshot of what is true about the variables at that moment (for example, “Sum currently holds the total of the numbers seen so far”). You do not fill a row for every line. You think through the logic: Analyse each step of the algorithm. Check: does it start in a valid state? Does it handle all possible cases? Are the conditions correct? If the loop is correct at the start of an iteration, does it remain correct at the end?
topics.urdu: مرحلہ وار استدلال میں الگورتھم کو منطقی حصوں میں توڑ کر ہر مرحلے پر اس کی حالت (State) دیکھی جاتی ہے: کیا شروع درست ہے، کیا تمام صورتیں سنبھلی ہیں، کیا شرط صحیح ہے، اور کیا لوپ کے ہر چکر کے بعد بھی نتیجہ درست رہتا ہے۔ ایک سے N تک جمع کی مثال میں Sum شروع میں 0 ہے، لوپ 1 سے N تک چلتا ہے، اور N=0 پر جواب 0 ہی رہتا ہے۔

topics.title: 2.1.3 Comparing Trace Tables and Stepwise Reasoning
topics.learn: Both methods verify correctness, but they fit different situations depending on the complexity and length of the algorithm.
topics.urdu: ٹریس ٹیبل خرد بینی (Micro) سطح پر کام کرتا ہے: ہر لائن اور ہر قیمت۔ مرحلہ وار استدلال بڑی (Macro) سطح پر ڈیزائن اور حالت چیک کرتا ہے۔ چھوٹے لوپ اور مبتدیوں کے لیے ٹیبل بہتر ہے؛ ہزار بار چلنے والے لوپ یا بڑے سسٹم کے لیے استدلال بہتر ہے۔

Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: FeatureTrace tableStepwise reasoning Best forSmall algorithm blocks, complex loops, and beginners learning to track variables.Large systems, architectural logic, and abstract mathematical proofs. Effort requiredHigh. Very tedious and impractical if a loop runs 1,000 times.Moderate. Needs strong logical deduction and abstract thinking. Primary goalCatching syntax misinterpretations or specific arithmetic errors line by line.Catching conceptual or structural flaws in the overall design. LevelMicro-level (line by line). Checks exact values.Macro-level (logic blocks). Checks overall state. Trace table Micro-level Line by line Exact values Stepwise reasoning Macro-level Logic blocks Overall state Trace tables zoom in on values; stepwise reasoning zooms out on design. Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: which method would you pick? Worked example sketchnote 2: A 12-line loop that adds five heights. Use a trace table. The loop is short, you are a beginner, and you need the exact Total. Worked example sketchnote 3: A billing system with 40 functions. Use stepwise reasoning. You cannot fill 10,000 rows. You check each module’s start state, end state and edge cases. Worked example sketchnote 4: A loop from i = 1 to 1,000 that should produce Sum = 500500. Do not write 1,000 rows. Argue: “Sum starts at 0; each i is added once; final Sum = n(n+1)/2 = 1000×1001/2 = 500500.” That is stepwise reasoning. Then dry-run a tiny N (say 5) with a trace table if you want extra confidence. Yaad rakhna: Micro vs macro. Trace table = microscope (every cell). Stepwise reasoning = map (whole city). Beginners start with the microscope; designers need the map. Common mistake: Mistake: saying one method is “better” in every question. Fix: they have different jobs. For a short dry-run in the exam, draw the table. For “explain why the algorithm is correct for any N”, write stepwise reasoning. topics.title: 2.2 Evaluating the Clarity of an Algorithm
topics.learn: Clarity means an algorithm is easy to read, understand and modify. In many cases, evaluating clarity is even more important than making the algorithm slightly faster. A clear algorithm is easier to maintain, debug and extend over time. The two key aspects of clarity are:

In many cases, evaluating clarity is even more important than making the algorithm slightly faster. A clear algorithm is easier to maintain, debug and extend over time. Algorithm A finds the class average in 8 confusing lines with variables a, b, c. Algorithm B uses two named functions and takes the same number of additions. Both are O(n). topics.title: 2.2.1 Modularity
topics.learn: Modularity means breaking an algorithm into smaller, independent parts such as functions, classes or modules. This makes the algorithm more organised and easier to work with. How to evaluate modularity Single Responsibility Principle (SRP). Each module should focus on one specific task. If a function calculates a sum, prints a report and saves a file, it violates SRP. Coupling. Modules should be reusable in different contexts. Good modularity means loose coupling: a change in one part does not smash the others. Tight coupling is when two functions share so many hidden details that you cannot reuse one without the other. Abstraction. A well-designed algorithm hides complex implementation details. You can call a sorting function without knowing whether it uses Bubble Sort or Selection Sort inside.
topics.urdu: ماڈیولریٹی کا مطلب الگورتھم کو آزاد حصوں (فنکشن، کلاس، ماڈیول) میں توڑنا ہے۔ جانچ کے تین اصول: واحد ذمہ داری (SRP) یعنی ایک فنکشن ایک کام؛ ڈھیلی جڑت (Loose Coupling) تاکہ ایک حصہ بدلنے سے دوسرے نہ ٹوٹیں؛ اور تجرید (Abstraction) یعنی اندرونی تفصیل چھپا کر صرف کام منگوانا، جیسے سورٹ فنکشن بلائے بغیر یہ جانے کہ ببل ہے یا سلیکشن۔

This makes the algorithm more organised and easier to work with. Matlab یہ ہوا کہ How to evaluate modularity اگلی بات یہ ہے: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP). Each module should focus on one specific task. If a function calculates a sum, prints a report and saves a file, it violates SRP. Example سے سمجھو: Coupling. Modules should be reusable in different contexts. Good modularity means loose coupling: a change in one part does not smash the others. Tight coupling is when two functions share so many hidden details that you cannot reuse one without the other. یاد رکھنا: Abstraction. A well-designed algorithm hides complex implementation details. You can call a sorting function without knowing whether it uses Bubble Sort or Selection Sort inside. Worked example sketchnote 1: Worked example: average of an array. Worked example sketchnote 2: Poor modularity (monoblock) Worked example sketchnote 3: All logic sits in one block, so you cannot reuse the sum. Worked example sketchnote 4: Step 1: Start Step 2: Set A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] Step 3: Set n = 5 Step 4: Set total = 0 Step 5: Set avg = 0 Step 6: For I = 1 to n Step 7: total = total + A[I] Step 8: End For Step 9: avg = total / n Step 10: Print avg Step 11: End Worked example sketchnote 5: Good modularity (functions) Worked example sketchnote 6: Two clear functions: CalculateSum() and FindAverage(). Worked example sketchnote 7: Step 1: Start Step 2: Set A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] Step 3: Set n = 5 Step 4: Print FindAverage(A, n) Step 5: End Worked example sketchnote 8: Function FindAverage(A, n) Sum = CalculateSum(A, n) Avg = Sum / n Return Avg End Function Worked example sketchnote 9: Function CalculateSum(A, n) Set Total = 0 For I = 1 to n Total = Total + A[I] End For Return Total End Function Worked example sketchnote 10: SRP check: CalculateSum only adds; FindAverage only divides. Loose coupling: you can reuse CalculateSum to find a total without computing an average. Abstraction: the main algorithm just calls FindAverage and does not see the loop. Worked example sketchnote 11: The source pseudocode numbers array positions from 1. Python numbers them from 0, so the loop is for i in range(n). Yaad rakhna: SRP in one line: one function, one job. If you cannot name the function with a short verb-phrase (CalculateSum, FindAverage), it is doing too much. Common mistake: Mistake: copying the 1-based loop for I = 1 to n: total = total + A[I] into Python. Then A[1] skips the first item and A[5] crashes. Fix: in Python use for i in range(n) so the indices are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. topics.title: 2.2.2 Readability
topics.learn: Readability is how easily another person can understand the purpose and logic of an algorithm without running it. It is about how clear the text and the flow are. How to evaluate readability Naming conventions — consistent rules for names. Good names make an algorithm easier to search and understand. Bad: v = d / t Good: velocity = distance / time Self-documentation — the algorithm explains itself, so you need fewer comments. Meaningful names and clean formatting make the purpose obvious. Control-flow simplicity — keep the logic straightforward. Avoid deep nesting (IF inside IF inside IF), limit extra conditions, and keep each function on one task. Consistency — one style throughout: indentation, spacing, and casing (camelCase or snake_case). Then the logic stands out instead of the mess.

topics.title: 2.3 Assess Algorithm Efficiency
topics.learn: Algorithm efficiency is measured in terms of time and space — how fast it runs and how much memory it uses. The key considerations for assessing efficiency are: Number of steps (described with Big O notation). Number of conditions (IF decisions). Number of repetitions (loops).

topics.title: 2.3.1 Number of Steps (Big O Notation)
topics.learn: When we discuss efficiency we ask how performance changes as the input size n increases. Big O notation is a mathematical method used to describe how the running time (or memory) grows as n grows. We ignore small constants and keep the most important term: if an algorithm does 3n + 5 steps we write O(n). In computer science, log n almost always means log base 2 (how many times you can halve n until you reach 1).

topics.title: 2.3.2 Number of Conditions
topics.learn: Conditions (IF statements) are decision points. Every condition forces the CPU to evaluate True or False, so excessive branching reduces performance. Computational cost. Each IF is extra work, even if the rest of the algorithm is simple. Nested conditions. IF inside IF often means a brute-force approach. It hurts both readability and speed. Short-circuiting (the optimisation goal). Stop evaluating as soon as the result is known. In a logical AND, if the first part is False the second part is skipped. In a logical OR, if the first part is True the second part is skipped.

topics.title: 2.3.4 The Efficiency Evaluation Framework
topics.learn: To evaluate an algorithm at a conceptual level, ask three questions: Does it scale? If n grows 10 times, does time jump 10 times (linear) or 100 times (quadratic)? Quadratic scaling fails for large datasets. What is the bottleneck? Focus on the most time-consuming section (usually the deepest loop) and try to improve that part. Is the cost worth it? A theoretically faster O(log n) algorithm can be too complex to code and maintain. For a list of just 50 items, a simple O(n) linear search is practically better because it is simple.

topics.title: 2.4 Refinements to improve clarity and efficiency
topics.learn: Improving an algorithm means reviewing it step by step: simplifying logic, removing redundant work, and picking smart data structures. A clear algorithm is easier to follow; an efficient one wastes fewer steps. Use meaningful names. Replace vague variables with descriptive ones. Bad: a = b / c. Good: average = totalSum / totalItems. Break into modules. Divide a massive block into functions, for example separating CalculateSum() from the printing logic. Improve structure and indentation. Packed loops and IF statements confuse the reader. Spacing reduces mental effort. Add comments. Keep them short. Explain why something is done, not just what is happening, especially for tricky logic. Reduce unnecessary steps. In Bubble Sort, after the first pass the largest value has settled at the end. Ignore that sorted tail on the next pass by shrinking the inner loop, and you save comparisons. Use better algorithms. Searching 1 million sorted records with Binary Search instead of Linear Search changes the time from seconds to milliseconds. Avoid re-computing values (memoization / caching). If a value never changes, compute it once outside the loop, store it, and reuse it. Use appropriate data structures. Direct access → array. Hierarchical data → tree. Do not force one structure everywhere.

topics.title: 2.5 Concept of Data Structure
topics.learn: A data structure is a systematic way of organising, storing and managing data so that an algorithm can access, modify and process it efficiently. Real-life analogy. Books on a shelf are arranged in a set order, so you can find a title quickly. Files in folders are grouped on purpose. Data structures do the same job inside computer memory.

topics.title: 2.5.1 Linear Data Structures: Array
topics.learn: An array holds a collection of similar items (the same data type) placed next to each other in contiguous memory (one continuous block). Each item has a position number called an index, usually starting from 0. Because the address of any cell can be calculated from the index, you can jump straight to it. That is direct access (also called random access), and it is O(1).

topics.title: Linear Data Structures: Linked List
topics.learn: A linked list stores data as a chain. Unlike an array, the items are not one continuous block. Each separate piece is a node sitting somewhere in memory. Each node has two parts: The first node is pointed to by HEAD. The last node’s link is NULL (nowhere). To find an item you start at HEAD and follow links one by one — sequential access, O(n). Real-life example: browser history. Clicking Back follows the pointer to the previous page-node. the actual data; a link (pointer) holding the memory address of the next node.

topics.title: Linear Data Structures: Stack
topics.learn: A stack is a linear data structure that works on the LIFO principle: Last-In, First-Out. The last element added is the first one removed. You cannot pull an item from the bottom or the middle. A TOP pointer always names the current top item. Real-life example: Undo in a text editor. Every action is piled on the stack; Undo POPs the most recent action first. PUSH — add an item to the top. POP — remove the item from the top.

topics.title: Linear Data Structures: Queue
topics.learn: A queue organises data on the FIFO principle: First-In, First-Out. Whoever arrives first is served first. Order truly matters. Real-life example: several documents sent to a printer. The printer prints the first document received, then the next. ENQUEUE — add an element at the Rear (back). DEQUEUE — remove an element from the Front.

topics.title: 2.5.2 Non-Linear Data Structures: Tree
topics.learn: A tree organises data in a hierarchy. Everything branches out from a single starting point called the root. It creates a strict one-to-many (parent–child) relationship. That is an excellent way to show how roles flow in an organisation. Real-life examples: a family tree (grandparents → parents → children) and folders inside folders on a drive.

topics.title: Non-Linear Data Structures: Graph
topics.learn: A graph organises data when things connect in a flexible, complex way. Unlike a tree, there is no strict hierarchy: any node can connect to any other node. Examples: Facebook friends; GPS mapping (the fastest route between two cities). Nodes (vertices) — the items (cities, people). Edges — the connections (roads, friendships).

topics.title: 2.6 Identify data structures in problem scenarios
topics.learn: To pick a structure, first see how the data is organised. If each item has a clear “before and after”, it is linear. If it branches or connects to many items, it is non-linear. Storing student grades for a class → Array. You usually know how many students there are, and all grades are the same type. Indices give rapid lookup. Music playlist / browser history → Linked list. Every song knows what comes next. When one finishes, follow the pointer. Frequent insert/delete is cheap. Undo or Redo → Stack (LIFO). Each typing or formatting action is PUSHed. Undo POPs the most recent action. Printer task scheduling → Queue (FIFO). Documents print in the exact order they were received. First-come, first-served. Organisational chart of a college → Tree. Principal is the root, then deans, then HODs, then teachers. Clear parent–child links. GPS navigation and maps → Graph. Cities are nodes, roads are edges. No strict top-down hierarchy. Several routes can reach the same destination.

topics.title: 2.7 Trace data retrieval in Array, List and Queue
topics.learn: Tracing data retrieval means following the step-by-step path of how an algorithm finds or accesses data. Array, linked list and queue are all linear, but the effort to find an item is very different because of how they are organised inside.

topics.title: 3.1 Data Structures in Python
topics.learn: A data structure is a way of organising values in a program so you can store them, find them and change them. Every useful program is built on data structures. Python gives you two layers: Python has these four abstract structures built in. You do not install anything extra. That is why collecting marks, names or settings is simpler in Python than in many other languages. Primitive data structures — the basic types that hold one value. Examples: integers (int), floating-point numbers (float), and booleans (bool). Abstract data structures — higher-level containers built from primitive types so you can hold many values and run richer operations. Examples: lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries.

topics.title: 3.1.1 Lists (Ordered, Mutable, Methods)
topics.learn: A list is Python’s most versatile built-in data structure. It stores an ordered collection of items in a single variable. Lists are mutable (you can change them after you create them) and they are written with square brackets []. Why use a list? One variable can hold thousands of values. You can mix types if you need to. You can add, remove and sort items as the program runs.

topics.title: 3.1.2 Tuples (Ordered, Immutable)
topics.learn: A tuple is an ordered collection that is immutable — once created, you cannot add, remove or replace items. Think of it as a read-only list. Tuples use parentheses (). Like lists, they allow duplicates, mixed types, and indexing from 0 (including negative indices).

topics.title: 3.1.3 Sets (Unordered, Unique, Math Operations)
topics.learn: A set stores an unordered, unindexed collection of unique elements. It is inspired by mathematical sets. You write a set with curly braces {}. Duplicates are removed as soon as the set is created. Because there is no index, myset[0] is illegal. The set itself is mutable (you can add and remove items). Each item inside must be immutable (numbers, strings, tuples of immutables — not lists).

topics.title: 3.1.4 Dictionaries (Key-Value Pairs)
topics.learn: A dictionary stores data as key–value pairs. It works like a real dictionary: you look up a word (the key) to find its meaning (the value). Write a dictionary with curly braces, and put a colon between each key and value. Ordered (Python 3.7+): insertion order is kept. Mutable: you can add, change and delete pairs. Keys are unique: if you repeat a key, the last value silently overwrites the earlier one. Values may repeat.
topics.urdu: ڈکشنری (Dictionary) کلید اور قدر (Key-Value) کے جوڑوں میں ڈیٹا رکھتی ہے۔ کلید منفرد ہوتی ہے؛ دہرائی ہوئی کلید پر آخری قدر رہ جاتی ہے۔ d[key] غیر موجود کلید پر KeyError دیتا ہے، جبکہ d.get(key, default) محفوظ ہے۔ .keys()، .values() اور .items() سے گھما جا سکتا ہے۔ فہرست انڈیکس سے، ڈکشنری کلید سے پہچانی جاتی ہے۔

Matlab یہ ہوا کہ Ordered (Python 3.7+): insertion order is kept. اگلی بات یہ ہے: Mutable: you can add, change and delete pairs. Example سے سمجھو: Keys are unique: if you repeat a key, the last value silently overwrites the earlier one. Values may repeat. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: KEY "name" → VALUE "Alice" You never search a dictionary by position. You search by key. A school analogue: a roll number (key) can point to only one student (value). If you assign that roll number to someone else, the old link is gone. Adding, changing and deleting d = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30} print(d) d["age"] = 31 print(d) d["city"] = "NYC" print(d) del d["city"] print(d) {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30} {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 31} {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 31, 'city': 'NYC'} {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 31} Assigning to an existing key updates the value. Assigning to a new key adds a pair. del d["city"] removes that pair. The duplicate-keys rule. Python does not crash. The last assignment wins. d = {"a": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3} print(d) {'a': 3} Accessing values safely 1. Direct brackets (risky) dict[key] works if the key exists. If it is missing, the program crashes with KeyError. 2. .get() (safe) dict.get(key) returns None if the key is missing. You may pass a default: dict.get(key, 0). person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30} print(person["name"]) print(person.get("salary")) print(person.get("salary", 0)) print("name" in person) print("salary" in person) Alice None 0 True False The oper Worked example sketchnote 1: Same data, four structures. Three subject marks: Worked example sketchnote 2: List [80, 70, 90] — easy to append a fourth test. Worked example sketchnote 3: Tuple (80, 70, 90) — a frozen result slip. Worked example sketchnote 4: Set {80, 70, 90} — unique scores only; two papers of 80 would become one 80. Worked example sketchnote 5: Dictionary {"math": 80, "eng": 70, "cs": 90} — you ask “What is CS?” and get 90 without remembering an index. Yaad rakhna: Keys are unique, like roll numbers. Values are the student records and may repeat (two students can both score 80). Memory: “get is gentle, brackets can break.” Common mistake: Older notes (and the chapter summary in some slides) still call dictionaries “unordered.” From Python 3.7 onwards insertion order is preserved, so you may write “ordered since 3.7.” Keys must be immutable: a list cannot be a key; a tuple of numbers can. Do not write {} when you want an empty set. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: FunctionPurposeWorks on min()Smallest element (numeric or alphabetical)List, tuple, set, dictionary keys max()Largest elementList, tuple, set, dictionary keys len()Number of elements (for a dict: number of keys)List, tuple, set, dictionary sum()Adds numeric elementsList, tuple, set, dictionary values via sum(d.values()) sorted()Returns a new sorted list; original unchangedList, tuple, set, dictionary keys s = {5, 1, 9, 3, 7} print(len(s)) print(min(s)) print(max(s)) print(sum(s)) print(sorted(s)) 5 1 9 25 [1, 3, 5, 7, 9] 5 + 1 + 9 + 3 + 7 = 25. sorted(s) always returns a list, even when the input is a set. topics.title: 3.1.6 Activity: Student Attendance System
topics.learn: Teachers need a quick way to mark who is in class. This program stores names in a list, asks about each student, counts how many said yes, and prints a summary with len().
topics.urdu: حاضری کا پروگرام طلبہ کے نام ایک فہرست میں رکھتا ہے، ہر نام کے لیے پوچھتا ہے، اور yes پر شمار کار (Counter) ایک بڑھاتا ہے۔ کل طلبہ len(students) سے، غیر حاضر کل − حاضر سے نکلتے ہیں۔ شمار کار لوپ سے پہلے صفر ہونا چاہیے۔

This program stores names in a list, asks about each student, counts how many said yes, and prints a summary with len(). Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: Store names in a list→Ask present? for each→Count yes→Print totals students = ["Ali", "Sara", "Ayesha"] present_count = 0 print("--- Attendance System ---\n") for student in students: status = input(f"Is {student} present? (yes/no): ").lower() if status == "yes": present_count += 1 print("\n--- Attendance Summary ---") print("Total Students:", len(students)) print("Students Present:", present_count) print("Students Absent:", len(students) - present_count) Worked example sketchnote 1: Sample run. Ali yes, Sara no, Ayesha yes. .lower() means YES or Yes still counts as present. Worked example sketchnote 2: Absent = len(students) - present_count = 3 − 2 = 1. The counter must start at 0 before the loop. If you put present_count = 0 inside the loop, the count would reset for every student. Yaad rakhna: Counter pattern: start at 0, loop, add 1 when a condition is true. You will reuse this in the word-frequency program (add 1 per word) and the grade tracker (add each mark). Common mistake: Only the exact string "yes" after .lower() counts as present. "y" or "present" is treated as absent. In a longer program you could also accept "y"; this activity keeps the rule simple. topics.title: 3.1.7 Activity: Word Frequency Counter
topics.learn: Count how many times each word appears in a sentence. This is a classic use of a dictionary plus .get(): the word is the key, the count is the value.
topics.urdu: جملے کو .split() سے الفاظ کی فہرست بناتے ہیں، پھر ہر لفظ ڈکشنری میں کلید ہوتا ہے اور اس کی گنتی قدر۔ نئے لفظ کے لیے .get(word, 0) + 1 سے گنتی 1 سے شروع ہوتی ہے۔ max(..., key=word_freq.get) سب سے زیادہ بار آنے والا لفظ دیتا ہے۔
topics.spokenUrdu: Students, السلام علیکم۔ آج کا lecture sketchnote Urdish میں ہے — poori topic ki in-depth explanation. Urdish یعنی class والی language: بات Urdu میں، computer کی terms English میں — formal Urdu ترجمہ نہیں۔ Topic کا title ہے: 3.1.7 Activity: Word Frequency Counter۔ یہ chapter Programming Fundamentals سے ہے۔ Sketchnote پر diagrams، tables، formulae aur har point ki depth دیکھتے رہو۔ Big idea Urdish میں: جملے کو .split() سے الفاظ کی فہرست بناتے ہیں، پھر ہر لفظ ڈکشنری میں کلید ہوتا ہے اور اس کی گنتی قدر۔ نئے لفظ کے لیے .get(word, 0) + 1 سے گنتی 1 سے شروع ہوتی ہے۔ max(..., key=word_freq.get) سب سے زیادہ بار آنے والا لفظ دیتا ہے۔ Ab sketchnote ki poori lecture Urdish میں سنو۔ دیکھو، sketchnote پہ لکھا ہے: Count how many times each word appears in a sentence. This is a classic use of a dictionary plus .get(): the word is the key, the count is the value. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: sentence = "python is easy python is fun python is powerful" words = sentence.split() word_freq = {} for word in words: word_freq[word] = word_freq.get(word, 0) + 1 print(f"Sentence: '{sentence}'\n") print("Word Frequency Table:") for word, count in word_freq.items(): print(f"{word:<10} : {count}") top_word = max(word_freq, key=word_freq.get) print(f"\nMost Frequent: '{top_word}' ({word_freq[top_word]} times)") Worked example sketchnote 1: Logic, step by step. Worked example sketchnote 2: Here python and is both occur 3 times. max returns 'python' because it appears first in the dictionary. Worked example sketchnote 3: sentence.split() cuts on spaces and gives['python', 'is', 'easy', 'python', 'is', 'fun', 'python', 'is', 'powerful']. Worked example sketchnote 4: For a new word, word_freq.get(word, 0) is 0, then you store 0 + 1 = 1. Worked example sketchnote 5: For a word already in the dictionary, .get(word, 0) returns the current count, then you add 1. Worked example sketchnote 6: {word:<10} pads the word to 10 characters so the colons line up. Worked example sketchnote 7: max(word_freq, key=word_freq.get) picks the key whose value is largest. If two words share the top count, max returns the first of those keys in insertion order. Yaad rakhna: The heart of every counter is one line: d[item] = d.get(item, 0) + 1. You can count letters, roll numbers or votes with the same pattern. Common mistake: This program is case-sensitive and space-based. "Python" and "python" would be two keys. Punctuation such as easy. would not match easy. For a class exercise, keep the sentence lowercase with spaces only, as here. If you wrote word_freq[word] += 1 without .get on a new word, you would get KeyError. topics.title: 3.2 Functions in Python
topics.learn: When the same instructions are written again and again, that is duplicate code. Duplicate code makes a program longer, harder to read, and painful to update (you must fix every copy). A function lets you write the instructions once and run them whenever you call the function’s name.
topics.urdu: فنکشن (Function) ہدایات کا وہ بلاک ہے جو ایک بار لکھا جاتا ہے اور بار بار بلایا جا سکتا ہے۔ اس سے کوڈ مختصر، ماڈیولر اور آسان اصلاح والا بنتا ہے۔ تعریف def سے شروع ہوتی ہے، نام اور پیرامیٹرز قوسین میں ہوتے ہیں، جسم انڈینٹ ہوتا ہے، اور return نتیجہ واپس بھیج سکتا ہے۔ تعریف کرنے سے فنکشن چلتا نہیں جب تک آپ اسے کال نہ کریں۔

Urdish یعنی class والی language: بات Urdu میں، computer کی terms English میں — formal Urdu ترجمہ نہیں۔ Topic کا title ہے: 3.2 Functions in Python۔ یہ chapter Programming Fundamentals سے ہے۔ Sketchnote پر diagrams، tables، formulae aur har point ki depth دیکھتے رہو۔ یہ Golden topic ہے۔ Board exam میں زیادہ marks اسی سے آتے ہیں۔ دھیان سے سنو۔ Big idea Urdish میں: Function ہدایات کا وہ بلاک ہے جو ایک بار لکھا جاتا ہے اور بار بار بلایا جا سکتا ہے۔ اس سے کوڈ مختصر، ماڈیولر اور آسان اصلاح والا بنتا ہے۔ تعریف def سے شروع ہوتی ہے، نام اور پیرامیٹرز قوسین میں ہوتے ہیں، جسم انڈینٹ ہوتا ہے، اور return نتیجہ واپس بھیج سکتا ہے۔ تعریف کرنے سے فنکشن چلتا نہیں جب تک آپ اسے کال نہ کریں۔ Ab sketchnote ki poori lecture Urdish میں سنو۔ دیکھو، sketchnote پہ لکھا ہے: When the same instructions are written again and again, that is duplicate code. Duplicate code makes a program longer, harder to read, and painful to update (you must fix every copy). A function lets you write the instructions once and run them whenever you call the function’s name. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: BenefitMeaning Code reusabilityWrite once, use anywhere. ModularityBreak a big problem into small named tasks. ReadabilityShorter, cleaner files with meaningful names. MaintainabilityFix a bug in one place and every call is fixed. def greet(): print("Hello, World!") greet() greet() Hello, World! Hello, World! The body is written once. Two calls run it twice. To change the message you edit one line inside greet. Key components of a function def→name→parameters→indented body→return (optional) Keyword — Python uses def to start a definition. Function name — the identifier you call, e.g. greet. Parameters — input names inside the parentheses. When you call the function, the values you pass are called arguments. Body — the indented block that runs on each call. Return statement — sends a result back to the caller (3.2.2). def add(a, b): print(f"Adding {a} + {b}") return a + b result = add(4, 6) print(result) Adding 4 + 6 10 Here a and b are parameters. 4 and 6 are arguments. return a + b sends 10 back, and that 10 is stored in result. Worked example sketchnote 1: Without a function you would copy the print-and-add lines every time you needed a sum. With a function, a new sum is one call: add(10, 20), add(1.5, 2.5). Yaad rakhna: DRY — Don’t Repeat Yourself. If you are about to copy-paste a block, wrap it in def. Name functions with verbs: greet, add, save_grades. Common mistake: Defining is not calling. After def greet(): nothing prints until you write greet(). Forgetting the parentheses — writing greet alone — does not run the body. The body must be indented; a line at column 0 is outside the function. Exam میں یہ terms English میں ہی لکھو: duplicate code, function, once, Without a function۔ ان کا مکمل Urdu ترجمہ examiner نہیں مانگتا۔ Board پہ سوال یوں آتا ہے: Write the four benefits (reusability, modularity, readability, maintainability) as separate bullets — that is a standard short question. For long questions, define a function, label def, name, parameters, body and return, then show one call. “What is duplicate code and how do functions solve it?” is also common. topics.title: 3.2.1 Types of Functions (Built-in vs User-defined)
topics.learn: There are two main types of functions in Python. a) Built-in functions are already defined by Python. You just call them. Examples you have already used: len(), range(), sum(), print(), input(), min(), max(), sorted(), int(), float(), type(). b) User-defined functions are functions you create with def for tasks that no built-in covers in one step — greeting a user, dividing with a zero check, writing a grade file.

topics.title: 3.2.2 Functions with Return Values
topics.learn: A function can either print a result (show it on the screen) or return a result (send it back to the caller). A returned value can be stored in a variable, printed later, or used in a further calculation. The call is replaced by the returned value, as if you had written that value in its place.
topics.urdu: return نتیجہ کال کرنے والے پروگرام کو واپس بھیجتا ہے تاکہ وہ متغیر میں محفوظ ہو سکے یا آگے حساب میں لگے۔ اگر return نہ ہو تو فنکشن None دیتا ہے۔ print صرف اسکرین پر دکھاتا ہے؛ اس سے حاصل شدہ قیمت دوبارہ استعمال نہیں ہوتی۔

A returned value can be stored in a variable, printed later, or used in a further calculation. The call is replaced by the returned value, as if you had written that value in its place. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: def multiply(a, b): return a * b result = multiply(5, 3) print("The answer is:", result) The answer is: 15 multiply(5, 3) evaluates to 15. That 15 is stored in result. Worked example sketchnote 1: Print versus return. This is the difference examiners want. Worked example sketchnote 2: show_sum prints 5 inside the function, then returns None (the default when there is no return). You cannot double that answer later. give_sum hands 5 back, so y * 2 is 10. Use print for messages; use return for results the rest of the program still needs. Yaad rakhna: return = send back; print = show now. return also exits the function immediately. Lines after return in the same function do not run. Common mistake: Writing print(a * b) inside multiply and then result = multiply(5, 3) stores None in result, not 15. If you later write result + 1 you get TypeError. Return the number; let the caller decide whether to print it. topics.title: 3.2.3 Activity: Arithmetic Calculator Using Functions
topics.learn: Each arithmetic operation is a separate function. That is modularity: addition is one small task, division is another (with a guard against dividing by zero). The main program only asks for two numbers and calls the functions.
topics.urdu: کیلکولیٹر میں ہر عمل الگ فنکشن ہے: جمع، تفریق، ضرب، تقسیم۔ یہ ماڈیولریٹی ہے۔ تقسیم سے پہلے صفر کی جانچ ضروری ہے ورنہ پروگرام رک جاتا ہے۔ input() سے ملنے والی تار کو float() سے عدد بنانا لازمی ہے ورنہ جمع جوڑنے کے بجائے الفاظ جوڑ دے گی۔

That is modularity: addition is one small task, division is another (with a guard against dividing by zero). The main program only asks for two numbers and calls the functions. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: def add(a, b): return a + b def subtract(a, b): return a - b def multiply(a, b): return a * b def divide(a, b): if b != 0: return a / b else: return "Cannot divide by zero" num1 = float(input("Enter first number: ")) num2 = float(input("Enter second number: ")) print("Addition:", add(num1, num2)) print("Subtraction:", subtract(num1, num2)) print("Multiplication:", multiply(num1, num2)) print("Division:", divide(num1, num2)) Worked example sketchnote 1: Sample run with 12 and 4. float is used so decimals work; even whole numbers print with a decimal (12 becomes 12.0). Worked example sketchnote 2: Check: 12 + 4 = 16, 12 − 4 = 8, 12 × 4 = 48, 12 ÷ 4 = 3. In Python 3, / always produces a float, so 3.0 not 3. Worked example sketchnote 3: Zero divisor: Worked example sketchnote 4: Without the if b != 0 test, 10 / 0 would raise ZeroDivisionError and stop the program. Yaad rakhna: Four functions, four names: add, subtract, multiply, divide. The main program should look like a contents page — a sequence of calls — not a pile of formulae. Common mistake: input() returns a string. If you skip float() (or int()), add would concatenate: "12" + "4" is "124". Convert first. Also, divide returns either a number or a string; do not later do arithmetic on the error message. topics.title: 3.2.4 Scope of Local and Global Variables
topics.learn: Scope is the region of a program where a variable can be seen and used. Python has two scopes you must know for this chapter. i) Local scope. A local variable is created inside a function. It exists only while that function is running. The main program cannot read it. ii) Global scope. A global variable is created outside all functions. Any function may read it, and the main program can use it too.
topics.urdu: دائرہ کار (Scope) بتاتا ہے کہ متغیر کہاں دکھائی دیتا ہے۔ لوکل متغیر فنکشن کے اندر بنتا ہے اور فنکشن ختم ہوتے ہی غائب ہو جاتا ہے؛ باہر سے پڑھنے پر NameError آتا ہے۔ گلوبل متغیر تمام فنکشنز سے باہر بنتا ہے اور اندر سے پڑھا جا سکتا ہے۔ فنکشن کے اندر اسی نام کو نئی قدر دینے سے نیا لوکل بنتا ہے، گلوبل نہیں بدلتا۔

topics.title: 3.3 & 3.4 File Handling and Operations (Modes r, w, a)
topics.learn: File handling is a program’s ability to create, read, write, update and delete files on disk. Variables live in RAM and vanish when the program ends. Files live on a hard disk or SSD and stay there — they are persistent.

topics.title: 3.6 The with Statement (Context Manager)
topics.learn: It is easy to forget .close(). If the program crashes before .close() runs, the file may be incomplete or corrupted. Python’s with statement is a context manager: it opens the file, runs the indented block, and always closes the file when the block ends — even if an error occurs inside.

topics.title: 3.8 Errors and Exceptions (Try-Except)
topics.learn: An exception is an error raised while the program is running — for example opening a file that is not there. Without handling, Python prints a traceback and stops. A try/except block catches the error and lets you show a clear message instead of crashing.
topics.urdu: ایکسپشن (Exception) چلتے پروگرام کی غلطی ہے، جیسے غیر موجود فائل کھولنا۔ try میں خطرناک کوڈ لکھیں اور except FileNotFoundError میں صاف پیغام دکھائیں تاکہ پروگرام کریش نہ ہو۔ پیشہ ورانہ سافٹ ویئر صارف کو سرخ ٹریس بیک کی بجائے سمجھ آنے والا جملہ دکھاتا ہے۔

Without handling, Python prints a traceback and stops. A try/except block catches the error and lets you show a clear message instead of crashing. Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: Error typeMeaning FileNotFoundErrorThe path does not exist. PermissionErrorThe operating system will not let you read or write that file. IOErrorA general input/output problem (disk full, disk disconnected). Put risky code in try. Put the recovery in except ErrorType. A final except Exception as e can catch anything else, using e as the error object. try: with open('missing_data.txt', 'r') as f: content = f.read() print(content) except FileNotFoundError: print("Error: The file does not exist. Please check the name.") except Exception as e: print(f"An unexpected error occurred: {e}") Error: The file does not exist. Please check the name. Without try, the same open raises: Traceback (most recent call last): File "missing.py", line 1, in <module> open('missing_data.txt', 'r') FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing_data.txt' Worked example sketchnote 1: When the file exists, the except blocks are skipped. Worked example sketchnote 2: Professional software does not dump a red traceback on a user. If a file is missing or a disk fails, the user should see a calm sentence such as “Please check the file name” or “Please try again later.” Yaad rakhna: try = attempt; except = backup plan. Catch the specific error first (FileNotFoundError), then a general Exception if you need it. Order matters: a bare except Exception first would swallow the specific error. Common mistake: Do not wrap your entire program in one silent except: that ignores every mistake. You would hide real bugs. Catch the errors you expect, and keep the message honest. 'w' and 'a' create a missing file, so they do not raise FileNotFoundError; 'r' does. Nine steps you must be able to write from memory: Board sketches aur tables bhi sketchnote کا part ہیں: import sqlite3 conn = sqlite3.connect("school.db") # 1–2 driver + connection cur = conn.cursor() # 3 cursor cur.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS students (id INTEGER, name TEXT, marks INTEGER)") cur.execute("INSERT INTO students VALUES (1, 'Ali', 85)") conn.commit() # 6 SAVE or the row vanishes cur.execute("SELECT * FROM students") rows = cur.fetchall() for r in rows: print(r) conn.close() # 9 unlock the file (1, 'Ali', 85) StepWhy it matters connectCreates the file if it does not exist cursorVehicle that carries SQL executeRuns one SQL command commitWrites INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to disk fetchallBrings SELECT results into a Python list of tuples closeFrees memory and unlocks the file Yaad rakhna: Strings inside SQL use single quotes: 'Ali'. Python strings around the SQL use double quotes (or a triple-quoted string). Common mistake: Forgetting commit() is the classic bug: the program prints nothing next time because the insert was never saved. Forgetting close() can lock school.db so the next run fails. topics.learn: Descriptive statistics squeeze a long list into a few honest numbers. Central tendency asks “what is typical?”. Spread asks “how mixed is the list?”.
